lessons.title: Why distributed systems are hard
lessons.summary: Partial failure, unreliable networks and clocks, the eight fallacies, and why the Two Generals problem has no solution.
lessons.body:
A distributed system is a set of computers that cooperate over a network and, ideally, look like one machine to the user. You build one because a single machine can't give you enough capacity, availability or geographic reach.

The price is that you inherit a class of problems that simply do not exist inside one process. Almost every technique in this module (quorums, consensus, fencing tokens, sagas, CRDTs) exists to tame one of the problems in this lesson.

## Partial failure

On a single computer, failure is mostly *total*: the process crashes, the kernel panics, the power goes. A program either runs or it doesn't, and that makes it easy to reason about.

In a distributed system, failure is **partial**. Some nodes work, some don't, and some are in an unknown state. Worse, failures are **non-deterministic**: the same request might succeed, fail, or hang.

Consider a client calling a remote service:

```
Client                  Server
  |---- request ------->|
  |                     |  (does work?)
  |       ...           |
  |   (no reply)        |
  |                     |
 timeout!
```

When the timeout fires, the client has no idea which of these happened:

1. The request was lost before reaching the server.
2. The server is down or paused (e.g. a long GC pause).
3. The server processed the request, but the reply was lost.
4. The server is just slow and will reply in 5 seconds.

All four look identical to the client. Cases 1 and 3 are the dangerous pair: in case 1 nothing happened, while in case 3 the side effect (charging a card, sending an email) **already happened**. This is why retries must be designed with idempotency in mind: an idempotency key lets the server recognise and discard a duplicate.

> [!warning] The core uncertainty
> A remote node can't tell "dead" from "slow" from "network broken". All it ever has is "I haven't heard back yet". Every failure detector is a guess.

## Living with timeouts

Since a timeout is the only failure signal you get, its value is a real design decision.

- **Too short**: a slow but healthy node is declared dead. You fail over, retry or rebalance for nothing, and the extra work can make the overload that caused the slowness worse.
- **Too long**: a genuinely dead node stalls requests (and users) for the whole timeout before anything happens.

A common starting point is to set request timeouts a little above the latency percentile you're willing to give up on (say the p99.9 of healthy calls), rather than picking a round number. Failure detectors used for cluster membership go further and *adapt* to observed latency; lesson 8 covers the phi accrual detector.

### Retries need care too

Retrying after a timeout is natural, but naive retries cause their own outages:

- **Use the same idempotency key on every attempt.** A fresh key per attempt makes each retry look like a new request, which defeats the point.
- **Back off exponentially, with jitter.** If thousands of clients retry on the same schedule, they hit the recovering server in synchronised waves.
- **Retry at one layer only.** If three layers each make up to 3 attempts, one user request can become 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls at the bottom layer, just when it is least able to cope.

```
web (3 tries)
 -> api (3 tries each)  = 9
   -> db (3 tries each) = 27
```

## The network is asynchronous

Most real networks (Ethernet, IP, the internet) are **asynchronous packet networks**. They promise nothing about delivery time. A packet can be:

- dropped (a switch buffer overflows),
- delayed arbitrarily (queueing in switches, TCP retransmits, a busy receiver),
- duplicated (a retransmit after an ack was lost),
- reordered (different paths).

TCP hides drops, duplicates and reordering from you, but it cannot hide *delay*, and it cannot tell you whether the far side processed your data once the connection breaks.

Distributed systems theory names three timing models:

| Model | Assumption |
|---|---|
| Synchronous | Known upper bounds on delay and clock drift |
| Partially synchronous | Usually bounded, but bounds are sometimes violated |
| Asynchronous | No bounds at all |

Real systems are best described as **partially synchronous**: they behave well most of the time, then occasionally a link saturates or a VM is paused for 30 seconds. Algorithms like Raft are designed so that *safety* never depends on timing, and only *liveness* (making progress) needs the network to calm down.

### Network partitions

A **partition** is when the network splits nodes into groups that cannot talk to each other, even though every node is still running. They happen far more than people expect: misconfigured switches, a cut fibre, a firewall rule, a NIC dropping only inbound packets.

```
 Region A            Region B
+--------+   XXXX   +--------+
| n1  n2 |---XXXX---| n3  n4 |
+--------+   XXXX   +--------+
 both sides think the other is dead
```

This is exactly the situation CAP talks about: during a partition, each side either refuses some requests (choosing consistency) or accepts them and risks divergence (choosing availability). PACELC adds that even with no partition you trade latency against consistency.

## Unreliable clocks and process pauses

Every machine has its own quartz clock, and they drift (Google assumes up to 200 ppm, around 17 seconds a day if never corrected). NTP corrects them, but only to within a few milliseconds on a good LAN, and much worse over the internet. Clocks can even **jump backwards** when NTP steps them.

Processes can also pause without noticing:

- a stop-the-world garbage collection (seconds, occasionally minutes),
- a VM being live-migrated or its hypervisor stealing CPU,
- the OS swapping memory to disk,
- a laptop lid closing.

A paused thread resumes and carries on as if no time had passed. If it was holding a lease ("I'm the leader for 10 more seconds"), it may now act on a lease that expired long ago. Lesson 6 shows how fencing tokens defend against this.

## The eight fallacies of distributed computing

Peter Deutsch and colleagues at Sun Microsystems listed the false assumptions that newcomers make. Each one causes real outages.

| Fallacy | What goes wrong |
|---|---|
| The network is reliable | Lost requests, half-done operations |
| Latency is zero | Chatty APIs become slow over a WAN |
| Bandwidth is infinite | Large payloads saturate links |
| The network is secure | Unencrypted internal traffic is sniffed |
| Topology doesn't change | Hard-coded IPs break on failover |
| There is one administrator | Conflicting configs, firewalls |
| Transport cost is zero | Serialisation CPU, cross-AZ fees |
| The network is homogeneous | Mixed MTUs, protocols, versions |

> [!example] Latency is not zero
> A page that makes 50 sequential calls to a service in the same data centre (0.5 ms round trip) spends 25 ms on the network. Move that service to another region (80 ms round trip) and the same page takes 4 seconds. Nothing in the code changed.

## The Two Generals problem

This thought experiment proves that **no protocol over an unreliable channel can guarantee that two parties agree** to act together.

Two armies, A and B, camp on hills either side of a city. They win only if they attack at the same time. Their only means of communication is a messenger who must run through the valley, where they might be captured.

```
General A                General B
  |-- "attack at 9" ------>|
  |                        | got it, but
  |                        | does A know?
  |<----- "ack" -----------|
  | got ack, but does B    |
  | know I got it?         |
  |-- "ack of ack" ------->|
  |          ... forever   |
```

Suppose some protocol worked, and consider the *shortest* sequence of messages that results in both attacking. The last message in that sequence might be captured. Whoever sent it can't know whether it arrived, so the decision must not depend on it, meaning a shorter protocol also works. Repeat the argument and you reach zero messages, which obviously can't coordinate anything. Contradiction.

### What it means in practice

You can't get *certain* agreement over a lossy network, so real systems settle for something weaker:

- **Probabilistic confidence**: send many messengers; the chance all are lost shrinks quickly.
- **Idempotent retries**: keep retrying until acknowledged, and make repeats harmless.
- **Agreement among a majority**: consensus algorithms (lesson 5) don't need every node to know; a majority is enough, and they tolerate lost messages by retrying.

TCP's connection close runs into the same limitation: the final ACK can be lost, and the side that sent it can't know. That's one reason the `TIME_WAIT` state exists: it lingers so it can re-send the ACK if the peer re-sends its FIN.

> [!note] Two Generals vs Byzantine Generals
> Two Generals is about **unreliable messages** between honest parties. The Byzantine Generals problem is about **dishonest or arbitrarily faulty nodes**. Practical Byzantine fault tolerance (PBFT and its descendants) needs 3f + 1 nodes to tolerate f traitors; most data-centre systems assume nodes are honest and only tolerate crashes, needing 2f + 1.

## Fault models

When you read about an algorithm, check which faults it tolerates:

| Model | Node behaviour |
|---|---|
| Crash-stop | Fails by halting, never returns |
| Crash-recovery | Halts, may restart with its disk |
| Omission | Drops some messages |
| Byzantine | Anything, including lying |

Raft and Paxos assume crash-recovery with durable storage. Blockchains assume Byzantine. Choosing the model is a design decision: Byzantine tolerance is expensive and rarely needed inside one company's data centre.

The fine print matters. "Crash-recovery with durable storage" means a node that restarts still has everything it `fsync`ed. A node that comes back with an empty or rolled-back disk (a replaced VM, a disk cache that lied about flushing) has **amnesia**, and that falls outside the model: it can vote twice in the same term and break safety. Likewise, silent data corruption is closer to a Byzantine fault than a crash, which is why storage systems add checksums.

## Key takeaways
- Failure in distributed systems is partial and non-deterministic; a timeout tells you nothing about whether the work happened.
- Networks can drop, delay, duplicate and reorder messages; partitions split working nodes apart.
- Clocks drift and jump, and processes pause unexpectedly, so time-based reasoning is fragile.
- The eight fallacies are the assumptions that cause outages; latency and reliability are the most common.
- Timeouts are guesses: tune them from real latency, retry with the same idempotency key, back off with jitter and retry at one layer only.
- Two Generals proves certain agreement over a lossy channel is impossible; systems use retries, idempotency and majorities instead.
- Always ask which fault model an algorithm assumes: crash-stop, crash-recovery or Byzantine.

questions.prompt: Your payment service calls a card processor and the call times out after 5 seconds. What can the payment service conclude?

options.text: The card was not charged, so it is safe to retry blindly.
options.explanation: Wrong. The processor might have charged the card and only the reply was lost. A blind retry could charge the customer twice.

options.text: The processor is down and should be removed from rotation.
options.explanation: Wrong. A timeout can't distinguish a dead node from a slow one or a lost packet. Removing it on one timeout is a guess, not a conclusion.

options.text: Nothing certain: the request may or may not have been processed.
options.explanation: Correct. The request could have been lost, the processor could be slow or paused, or it processed the charge and the reply was lost. All look identical from the caller's side.

options.text: The card was charged, because the processor must have received the request.
options.explanation: Wrong. The request itself may have been dropped before arriving, in which case no charge happened.

questions.workedExample:
List the possibilities a timeout hides:

1. Request lost on the way: no charge.
2. Processor crashed or paused: maybe no charge, maybe partway.
3. Charge done, reply lost: **charged**.
4. Processor slow: will charge, reply arrives late.

All four look identical to the caller, and cases 1 and 3 have opposite side effects. So the only safe conclusion is uncertainty. The practical fix is an **idempotency key**: send the same key on retry, and the processor returns the original result instead of charging again.

questions.prompt: A page makes 40 **sequential** calls to a backend. Each call does 1 ms of work. The backend moves from the same data centre (0.5 ms round trip) to another region (70 ms round trip). Roughly how long does the page now spend on these calls?

options.text: About 2.8 seconds
options.explanation: Correct. 40 × (70 + 1) = 2,840 ms. Each sequential call pays the full round trip, so latency multiplies by call count.

options.text: About 60 ms
options.explanation: Wrong. This is the old figure: 40 × (1 + 0.5) = 60 ms. It ignores the new round-trip time.

options.text: About 110 ms
options.explanation: Wrong. This adds one 70 ms round trip to the old total, as if all calls shared one round trip. Sequential calls each pay the full latency.

options.text: About 28 seconds
options.explanation: Wrong by a factor of 10; it treats each round trip as 700 ms.

questions.workedExample:
Per call time = round trip + work.

- Before: 0.5 + 1 = 1.5 ms, × 40 = **60 ms**.
- After: 70 + 1 = 71 ms, × 40 = **2,840 ms**.

That is the fallacy "latency is zero" in action. Fixes: batch the 40 calls into one, run them in parallel (total ≈ 71 ms), or keep chatty services co-located.

questions.prompt: In the Two Generals problem, why doesn't adding an "ack of the ack" (and so on) solve it?

options.text: Because the generals might lie about receiving messages.
options.explanation: Wrong. That is the Byzantine Generals problem. In Two Generals both parties are honest; only the messenger is unreliable.

options.text: Because messages take too long, and the attack time passes.
options.explanation: Wrong. The impossibility holds even with unlimited time. The issue is loss, not delay.

options.text: Because it can be solved, but needs exactly three acknowledgements.
options.explanation: Wrong. No finite number of acknowledgements works; the proof shows any finite protocol can be shortened until it fails.

options.text: Because the last message sent can always be lost, and its sender can't know whether it arrived.
options.explanation: Correct. Whatever message is last, its sender is uncertain about it, so the decision can't depend on it. Removing it gives a shorter protocol with the same problem, all the way down to zero messages.

questions.workedExample:
Proof by contradiction:

1. Assume a protocol exists; take its shortest successful run of *k* messages.
2. The *k*th message might be captured. Its sender acts the same whether or not it arrived (they can't tell).
3. For agreement to be guaranteed, the receiver must also act the same without it. So *k − 1* messages suffice.
4. Repeat until *k = 0*: no messages can't coordinate an attack. Contradiction.

In practice systems accept probabilistic agreement (many messengers) or idempotent retries.

questions.prompt: Which of these can cause a healthy node to *appear* dead to its peers? Select all that apply.

options.text: A 20-second stop-the-world GC pause
options.explanation: Correct. The process can't send heartbeats during the pause, so peers time out, even though it will resume normally.

options.text: A network partition between it and the peers
options.explanation: Correct. The node is running and serving whichever side it can reach, but the other side hears nothing.

options.text: A saturated switch queue delaying heartbeats
options.explanation: Correct. Delay beyond the timeout is indistinguishable from death; the heartbeat arrives too late.

options.text: The node using TCP instead of UDP
options.explanation: Wrong. The transport protocol doesn't make a node look dead. TCP still suffers delays, but choosing it over UDP isn't a cause of false suspicion.

options.text: Its VM's hypervisor stealing CPU for a live migration
options.explanation: Correct. The guest is frozen during migration, much like a GC pause, and misses heartbeats.

questions.workedExample:
A peer decides "dead" when it hasn't heard from a node within a timeout. Anything that stops or slows messages for longer than that timeout causes a false positive:

- **Pauses** (GC, VM migration, swapping) stop the sender.
- **Partitions** stop the path.
- **Queueing** delays the path.

Transport choice isn't the issue. The lesson: failure detection is always a guess, which is why protocols must stay safe when the guess is wrong.

questions.prompt: You must tolerate up to **2** simultaneously faulty nodes. How many nodes do you need under a crash-fault model versus a Byzantine model?

options.text: Crash: 3, Byzantine: 5
options.explanation: Wrong. 3 nodes with 2 crashed leaves 1, which isn't a majority. Crash tolerance needs 2f + 1.

options.text: Crash: 5, Byzantine: 7
options.explanation: Correct. Crash faults need 2f + 1 = 5 so a majority (3) survives. Byzantine faults need 3f + 1 = 7 so honest nodes outvote liars even when some honest nodes are slow.

options.text: Crash: 4, Byzantine: 6
options.explanation: Wrong. Even sizes don't improve fault tolerance for majorities, and these miss the 2f + 1 and 3f + 1 bounds.

options.text: Crash: 5, Byzantine: 5
options.explanation: Wrong. Byzantine nodes can send conflicting messages to different peers, so you need extra honest nodes: 3f + 1 = 7.

questions.workedExample:
With f = 2:

- **Crash**: n = 2f + 1 = 5. If 2 crash, 3 remain, and 3 is a majority of 5, so quorums can still form and any two quorums overlap.
- **Byzantine**: n = 3f + 1 = 7. Quorums are 2f + 1 = 5. Two quorums overlap in at least 3 nodes, and at most 2 are traitors, so at least one honest node is in both.

This is why Raft clusters are 3 or 5 nodes and BFT systems are 4, 7, 10...

questions.prompt: A leader holds a 10-second lease. It checks the lease (8 s left), then hits a 15-second GC pause, then writes to storage. What is the problem, and what does it illustrate?

options.text: A stale leader may write after a new leader was elected: a process can't rely on its own sense of elapsed time.
options.explanation: Correct. The paused process doesn't notice time passing, so it acts on an expired lease. Storage must reject stale writers, e.g. with fencing tokens.

options.text: No problem: it checked the lease before writing.
options.explanation: Wrong. The check and the write are separated by the pause. By the time it writes, the lease expired 7 seconds earlier and another node may be leader.

options.text: The write is rejected automatically because GC pauses abort I/O.
options.explanation: Wrong. GC pauses don't abort anything; the thread resumes exactly where it left off and performs the write.

options.text: The problem is clock skew between the leader and storage.
options.explanation: Wrong. Clocks could be perfectly synchronised and this still happens; the issue is the pause between check and use.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline:

```
t=0   lease granted (to t=10)
t=2   check: 8 s left, OK
t=2   GC pause starts
t=10  lease expires; n2 elected
t=17  pause ends; old leader writes
```

At t=17 two nodes believe they are leader. This is a check-then-act race made worse by unbounded pauses. The defence (lesson 6) is a **fencing token**: storage remembers the highest token it has seen and rejects the old leader's lower one.

questions.prompt: Raft is described as never violating safety under any network timing, but needing a "well-behaved" network for liveness. Which timing model is this?

options.text: Synchronous
options.explanation: Wrong. A synchronous model assumes known bounds always hold; Raft explicitly stays safe when they don't.

options.text: Fully asynchronous with guaranteed termination
options.explanation: Wrong. FLP shows deterministic consensus can't guarantee termination in a fully asynchronous model with even one crash.

options.text: Partially synchronous
options.explanation: Correct. The system is usually timely but sometimes isn't. Safety holds always; progress happens once delays settle back within bounds, which matches real networks.

options.text: Byzantine
options.explanation: Wrong. Byzantine is a fault model (nodes lie), not a timing model, and Raft doesn't tolerate Byzantine nodes.

questions.workedExample:
Separate two properties:

- **Safety**: nothing bad happens (no two leaders commit conflicting entries). Raft guarantees this with terms and majority votes, regardless of timing.
- **Liveness**: something good eventually happens (a leader is elected). This needs timeouts to work, i.e. messages arriving within bounds *most* of the time.

That split is exactly the partially synchronous model, and it sidesteps FLP: termination is only promised in periods of good behaviour.

questions.prompt: Raft assumes a **crash-recovery** fault model with durable storage. Which of these failures fall **outside** that model, so Raft gives no safety guarantee if they happen? Select all that apply.

options.text: A node reboots after a power cut with its fsynced log intact.
options.explanation: Inside the model. Crash-recovery means exactly this: the node halts, restarts and still has everything it made durable. Raft handles it.

options.text: A node comes back on a fresh VM with an empty disk but the same identity.
options.explanation: Outside the model. This is amnesia: the node has forgotten its vote and its log, so it can vote twice in one term or help elect a leader missing committed entries.

options.text: A disk silently flips bits in a stored log entry.
options.explanation: Outside the model. Silent corruption makes a node report data it never received, which is closer to a Byzantine fault. Systems add checksums to turn it back into a detectable crash.

options.text: A node is paused for 30 seconds by the hypervisor.
options.explanation: Inside the model. A pause looks like a slow or temporarily crashed node. Raft stays safe; the node simply rejoins and learns about any newer term.

options.text: A disk controller acknowledges fsync but loses the write on power failure.
options.explanation: Outside the model. The node believes its vote or log entry is durable when it is not, so after a restart it can contradict what it promised. This is a known cause of real data loss.

questions.workedExample:
Ask of each failure: "does the node behave as a crashed node that restarts with all its durable state?"

| Failure | Behaves like |
|---|---|
| Reboot, disk intact | crash-recovery |
| Fresh disk, same id | amnesia |
| Bit flip | arbitrary (Byzantine-ish) |
| 30 s pause | slow node |
| Lying fsync | amnesia |

Only the first and fourth fit the model. The lesson: the fault model is a contract with your hardware and operations. If you replace a node, give it a **new identity** and add it through a membership change, rather than reusing the old one with an empty disk.

questions.prompt: Your cluster manager marks a node dead after **1 second** without a heartbeat and immediately moves its shards elsewhere. Nodes run a JVM that has occasional 2-second GC pauses under load. What is the most likely result during a traffic spike?

options.text: Faster recovery, because failures are detected within a second.
options.explanation: Wrong. Most of the "failures" detected are healthy nodes in a GC pause. Detecting them quickly just triggers needless work.

options.text: Nothing unusual: heartbeats are sent on a separate thread, so GC can't affect them.
options.explanation: Wrong. A stop-the-world pause halts every application thread, including the heartbeat sender.

options.text: Split brain is impossible because the timeout is short.
options.explanation: Wrong. A short timeout makes false suspicion more likely, not less. It does nothing to prevent two nodes acting on the same shard.

options.text: Flapping: healthy nodes are repeatedly declared dead, shards move back and forth, and the extra load causes more pauses.
options.explanation: Correct. A timeout shorter than normal pauses produces false positives. Each one triggers rebalancing work, which adds load, which causes more GC, a classic feedback loop.

questions.workedExample:
1. Under load, a node pauses for 2 s.
2. After 1 s the manager declares it dead and starts moving its shards (copying data, redirecting traffic).
3. At 2 s the node resumes, healthy, and finds its shards gone or contested.
4. The rebalancing traffic loads the surviving nodes, which then pause too.

Fixes:

- Set the timeout above normal pause and latency behaviour (measure it), or use an **adaptive** detector such as phi accrual.
- Add a grace period or a "suspect" state before acting.
- Rate-limit rebalancing so a burst of suspicions can't move everything at once.

questions.prompt: Node n1's network card starts dropping **inbound** packets but still sends outbound ones. n1 sends heartbeats to n2 and n3 as normal. What does each side conclude?

options.text: Everyone agrees n1 is down, because its network card is faulty.
options.explanation: Wrong. n2 and n3 keep receiving n1's heartbeats, so from their side n1 looks perfectly healthy.

options.text: n1 suspects n2 and n3 are dead, while n2 and n3 believe n1 is alive.
options.explanation: Correct. This is an asymmetric partition. n1 hears nothing, so it suspects everyone else. The others hear n1 fine, so they see no problem, even though n1 cannot receive their requests or replies.

options.text: n2 and n3 suspect n1, while n1 believes everything is fine.
options.explanation: Wrong, it's the other way round. Outbound traffic from n1 still works, so n2 and n3 hear it; n1 is the one hearing nothing.

options.text: Nobody notices anything, because TCP retransmits the lost packets.
options.explanation: Wrong. TCP retransmits, but every retransmission is dropped too. Connections into n1 stall and eventually time out.

questions.workedExample:
Draw the two directions separately:

```
n1 --> n2, n3   works
n1 <-- n2, n3   dropped
```

- n1: no heartbeats or replies arrive, so it times out on everyone.
- n2, n3: n1's heartbeats arrive on time, so it looks alive, yet requests they send to it never get answered.

Why it matters: if n1 is a leader, it may keep sending heartbeats that suppress elections while being unable to receive acknowledgements, so nothing commits. Partial and asymmetric failures (sometimes called **gray failures**) are why systems use end-to-end health checks (can you actually do work?) and indirect probes, rather than "did I hear a heartbeat?".

questions.prompt: A checkout client sends `POST /charges` with an idempotency key, times out, and retries. Which client design actually prevents double charges?

options.text: Generate a new random key on each attempt so the server can tell attempts apart.
options.explanation: Wrong. A new key makes every retry look like a brand-new charge, so the server will happily process it again. The key must identify the operation, not the attempt.

options.text: Generate one key per checkout, store it with the order, and reuse it on every retry.
options.explanation: Correct. The server stores the result against the key. A retry with the same key returns the original result instead of charging again, even if the first attempt did succeed.

options.text: Use the current timestamp as the key.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each retry happens at a different time, so the key changes, which is the same mistake as a random key per attempt.

options.text: Skip the key and wait longer before retrying.
options.explanation: Wrong. However long you wait, a timeout still can't tell you whether the first charge happened. Waiting only reduces how often the problem shows up.

questions.workedExample:
The key must be **the same for every attempt at the same logical operation**:

```
key = order.id + ":charge"
attempt 1 -> timeout (charged!)
attempt 2 -> server: seen key,
             return first result
```

Store the key with the order *before* the first attempt, so even a client crash and restart reuses it. On the server, record the key and the result atomically with the charge, otherwise a crash between them reopens the gap.

link.title: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs (AWS)

questions.prompt: A request passes through a web tier, an API tier and a database tier. Each tier makes **up to 3 attempts** on failure. The database starts timing out on every call. How many database calls can one user request now trigger, and what's the usual fix?

options.text: 9 calls; add jitter to the backoff.
options.explanation: Wrong count. 9 is the API tier's total (3 web attempts × 3 API attempts). Each of those makes 3 database attempts, giving 27. Jitter spreads retries out but doesn't reduce their number.

options.text: 3 calls; nothing needs fixing because only the database retries.
options.explanation: Wrong. Every tier retries independently, so the attempts multiply rather than add.

options.text: 27 calls; retry at a single layer and use retry budgets or circuit breakers.
options.explanation: Correct. 3 × 3 × 3 = 27. Retrying at one layer caps amplification at 3×, and a retry budget or circuit breaker stops retries entirely when the failure rate is high.

options.text: 81 calls; remove all retries.
options.explanation: Wrong. 81 would be four tiers. Removing every retry also throws away the benefit for brief, transient errors; the aim is to bound retries, not ban them.

questions.workedExample:
Multiply attempts down the stack:

| Tier | Attempts | Running total |
|---|---|---|
| Web | 3 | 3 |
| API | 3 each | 9 |
| DB | 3 each | **27** |

So a database that is already struggling receives 27× its normal load from the retries alone, which keeps it down. Standard practice:

1. Retry at **one** layer.
2. Exponential backoff with jitter.
3. A **retry budget** (e.g. retries may add at most 10% extra load) or a circuit breaker that fails fast when errors are widespread.

lessons.summary: What linearizable, sequential, causal and eventual consistency actually promise, plus the session guarantees users notice.
lessons.body:
When data is replicated, different clients can see different values at the same moment. A **consistency model** is a contract that says which histories of reads and writes are allowed. Stronger models allow fewer surprising histories, at a cost in latency and availability.

CAP's "C" means one specific model, linearizability. In practice there's a whole spectrum, and choosing the right point on it is one of the most important design decisions you make.

## The hierarchy

From strongest to weakest (these are models for individual reads and writes, not multi-step transactions):

```
   Linearizable
        |
   Sequential
        |
     Causal
```

Each level shown allows every history the level above allows, plus more. Session guarantees form additional, partly independent properties. Eventual convergence is a separate liveness promise and should not be inferred merely from a safety ordering model. Jepsen's map also places transactional models such as serializability alongside these.

## Linearizability

**Linearizability** (also called atomic or strong consistency) means the system behaves as if there were **one copy** of the data, and every operation takes effect **atomically at some instant between its start and its end**.

The key consequence is **recency**: once a write completes, every later read (in real time) must see it or something newer. And once any client has read a new value, no later read anywhere may return the old one.

```
time ------------------------------->
A: |--write x=1--|
B:                 |--read x--| -> 1
C:   |------read x------|        -> 0 or 1
```

C's read overlaps A's write, so either answer is fine. B's read starts after the write finished, so it **must** return 1.

### A violation

```
A: |--------write x=1--------|
B:    |-read-| -> 1
C:              |-read-| -> 0   ILLEGAL
```

B saw the new value; C started *after* B finished, yet saw the old one. That's what happens with naive async replication: B hit an up-to-date replica, C hit a lagging one.

### Composability

Linearizability is **local** (Herlihy and Wing call it *composable*): if every individual object is linearizable, the system as a whole is linearizable. You can shard keys across independent linearizable groups and still reason about each one alone. Sequential consistency does **not** compose: two objects that are each sequentially consistent can together produce a history that no single order explains.

### Where you need it

- **Leader election and locks**: everyone must agree who holds the lock.
- **Uniqueness constraints**: two users can't both claim username `alice`.
- **Cross-channel timing**: a user uploads a file, then a message on a queue tells a worker to process it. If the worker reads a stale replica, the file "doesn't exist".

### What it costs

Linearizability needs coordination (a single leader with synchronous confirmation, or consensus). Every read and write must reach a majority or the leader, so latency includes at least one round trip to them. During a partition, the minority side must stop serving. That's CAP, and PACELC's "else latency" is the cost even without partitions.

> [!note] Linearizable vs serializable
> **Serializability** is about *transactions* over many objects: the result equals *some* serial order, which needn't match real time. **Linearizability** is about *single operations* respecting real time. Having both is called **strict serializability**. Spanner (which calls it external consistency) and FoundationDB provide it; CockroachDB provides serializability with somewhat weaker real-time guarantees.

## Sequential consistency

**Sequential consistency** (Lamport, 1979) requires that all operations appear in *some* single total order that is consistent with **each client's program order**, but not necessarily with real time.

So in the violation diagram above, if B and C are different clients with no communication, sequential consistency could allow it (order: C reads 0, A writes 1, B reads 1). What it forbids is a single client seeing time go backwards, or two clients disagreeing about the order of two writes.

It's mostly of interest for CPU memory models and as a stepping stone. ZooKeeper is a real-world example of something close to it: writes are linearizable, but a read served by a follower may be stale, while each client still sees updates in one agreed order.

### Telling the three apart

The names are easy to mix up, so compare them on two questions: what do they cover, and do they respect real time?

| Model | Covers | Real time? |
|---|---|---|
| Linearizable | Single operations | Yes |
| Sequential | Single operations | No, only per-client order |
| Serializable | Multi-object transactions | No |
| Strict serializable | Transactions | Yes |

A quick test: if a history only looks wrong when you compare *wall-clock* times across different clients, it can still be sequentially consistent or serializable, but it isn't linearizable or strictly serializable.

## Causal consistency

**Causal consistency** only orders operations that are **causally related**. If operation A could have influenced operation B (B happened after reading A's result, or they're in the same session), everyone must see A before B. **Concurrent** operations can be seen in different orders by different nodes.

```
Alice: post "I lost my job"
Alice: post "Never mind, got a new one!"
Bob reads 2nd post, replies "Congrats!"

Causal: nobody sees "Congrats!" before
        the post it replies to.
```

Without causal consistency, Carol might see Bob's "Congrats!" before Alice's posts arrive, or see the posts in reverse, which reads as Bob celebrating a sacking.

Causal consistency is, in effect, the **strongest model that remains available during partitions**: each side keeps working and merges causal histories later. (Strictly, Mahajan et al. proved this for a slight strengthening called real-time causal, and it needs *sticky* availability, where each client keeps talking to the same replica.) Systems track causality with version vectors or dependency metadata; MongoDB offers causally consistent sessions.

## Eventual consistency

**Eventual consistency** promises only that if writes stop, all replicas *eventually* converge to the same value. It says nothing about what you read in the meantime: stale values, values going backwards, writes out of order.

It's what you get from Dynamo-style stores with low quorum settings, DNS, and asynchronous read replicas. It is cheap and highly available, and fine for things like like-counts and product views. But "eventually" has no bound, and convergence needs a conflict-resolution rule (lesson 8).

Some systems offer **bounded staleness** in between: reads may lag, but by no more than a stated time or number of versions (Azure Cosmos DB offers this as a named level). That is stronger than eventual, because it gives a bound, but weaker than linearizable.

## Session guarantees

Pure eventual consistency produces anomalies users notice immediately. Terry et al. (Bayou, 1994) defined four **session guarantees** that fix the worst of them cheaply, per client session:

| Guarantee | Promise |
|---|---|
| Read-your-writes | You see your own writes |
| Monotonic reads | You never see time go backwards |
| Monotonic writes | Your writes apply in order |
| Writes-follow-reads | Writes after a read are ordered after it |

### Read-your-writes

A user edits their profile, the page reloads from a lagging replica, and the edit has "vanished". They edit again. Read-your-writes prevents this.

Implementations:

- Read from the authoritative leader for relevant data, or track a confirmed replication position. Routing to the leader for 60 s is only a heuristic unless replica lag is bounded below that interval.
- The client remembers the log position (LSN / timestamp) of its last write; a replica serves the read only if it has caught up past that point.

### Monotonic reads

```
User refreshes comments twice:
  read 1 -> replica R1 (up to date)
            shows 10 comments
  read 2 -> replica R2 (lagging)
            shows 8 comments  <- went back
```

Fix: pin each user to a replica whose history never rolls back; when moving replicas, carry the last-seen version and wait for that version. Tracking versions is necessary across failover or rollback.

> [!tip] Session guarantees are cheap
> They need only per-client metadata, not global coordination. Cross-device sessions are harder: the phone doesn't know what the laptop wrote unless the token is shared via the server.

## Choosing a model

| Need | Model |
|---|---|
| Locks, leader, unique IDs | Linearizable |
| Comments, chat threads | Causal |
| Own profile edits | Read-your-writes |
| Like counts, view counts | Eventual |

A common pattern is to mix them: strong consistency for a small core (account balances, inventory reservation) and weaker models everywhere else.

> [!warning] Check the claims
> Jepsen has repeatedly found databases that advertise strong consistency but violate it under partitions or clock skew. Treat vendor claims as hypotheses and look for independent testing.

## Key takeaways
- A consistency model defines which read/write histories are allowed; stronger means fewer anomalies but more coordination.
- Linearizability = one copy, real-time order. Needed for locks, leader election and uniqueness; it costs latency and partition availability.
- Sequential consistency keeps per-client order but not real time; causal consistency orders only causally related operations.
- Linearizability composes across objects (you can shard it); sequential consistency doesn't.
- Causal consistency can preserve availability for clients that remain on a suitable replica (sticky availability); arbitrary client migration during a partition can require waiting for dependencies.
- Eventual consistency only promises convergence; add session guarantees (read-your-writes, monotonic reads) to avoid user-visible anomalies.
- Serializability (transactions) and linearizability (real-time single operations) are different; both together is strict serializability.

## Further reading
- [Consistency models map (Jepsen)](https://jepsen.io/consistency)
- [Linearizability (Jepsen)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/linearizable)
- [Causal consistency (Jepsen)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/causal)
- [Sequential consistency (Jepsen)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/sequential)
- [Strict serializability (Jepsen)](https://jepsen.io/consistency/models/strict-serializable)
- [Linearizability versus serializability (Peter Bailis)](https://www.bailis.org/blog/linearizability-versus-serializability/)
- [Please stop calling databases CP or AP (Kleppmann)](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2015/05/11/please-stop-calling-databases-cp-or-ap.html)

questions.prompt: A user updates their display name, the page reloads, and the old name appears. A second later it shows the new one. Which guarantee was violated?

options.text: Monotonic writes
options.explanation: Wrong. Monotonic writes is about a client's own writes being applied in order. Only one write happened here.

options.text: Read-your-writes
options.explanation: Correct. The user failed to see their own completed write, because the reload was served by a replica that hadn't yet received it.

options.text: Eventual consistency
options.explanation: Wrong. Eventual consistency was honoured: the replicas converged a second later. It just doesn't promise anything about the interim.

options.text: Writes-follow-reads
options.explanation: Wrong. That guarantee orders writes made after a read relative to what was read; this scenario is about reading after writing.

questions.workedExample:
1. The write went to the leader and succeeded.
2. The reload read from an async replica with replication lag.
3. The user saw a state older than their own write.

That is precisely a **read-your-writes** violation. Fixes: read the user's own data from the leader, or have the client send its last write position so the replica waits (or redirects) until it has caught up.

questions.prompt: Client A writes x=1 from 10:00:00.000 to 10:00:00.300. Client B reads x from 10:00:00.100 to 10:00:00.150 and gets **1**. Client C reads x from 10:00:00.200 to 10:00:00.250. Under **linearizability**, what can C's read return?

options.text: Only 1
options.explanation: Correct. B's read returned 1, so the write's linearization point is before 10:00:00.150. C starts at .200, after that point, so it must see 1 (or newer).

options.text: Either 0 or 1, because C's read overlaps A's write.
options.explanation: Wrong. Overlap alone would allow either, but B already observed 1 and finished before C started. Linearizability then forbids C going back to 0.

options.text: Only 0, because A's write hasn't finished yet.
options.explanation: Wrong. A write can take effect at any instant between its start and end. B already saw it take effect.

options.text: Anything, linearizability doesn't constrain concurrent reads.
options.explanation: Wrong. Linearizability constrains every operation relative to real time; reads that follow a read seeing the new value must also see it.

questions.workedExample:
Draw it:

```
A: |------write x=1------|
B:    |-r=1-|
C:            |-r=?-|
```

1. Each operation takes effect at a single instant within its interval.
2. B returned 1, so A's write took effect before B ended (.150).
3. C started at .200 > .150, so the write is already in effect for C.
4. C must return 1.

If C returned 0, the history would show the value going *backwards*, which no single copy could do.

questions.prompt: A user refreshes a comment thread and sees 12 comments, refreshes again and sees 9, then 12 again. Reads go round-robin to async replicas. What's the cheapest fix?

options.text: Make all replication synchronous.
options.explanation: Wrong for 'cheapest'. It would fix it, but makes every write wait for every replica and fails writes when one replica is down.

options.text: Run Raft consensus for every read.
options.explanation: Wrong. Consensus reads give linearizability, far stronger (and slower) than needed for this anomaly.

options.text: Pin each user's reads to the same replica (e.g. hash of user id).
options.explanation: Correct while the chosen replica keeps an advancing history. To preserve the guarantee through failover, carry the last-seen replication position and require the replacement to catch up.

options.text: Add a cache in front of the replicas with a 1-hour TTL.
options.explanation: Wrong. A cache hides changes for an hour and, if it misses, still reads from a random replica. It trades one anomaly for heavy staleness.

questions.workedExample:
The anomaly is reads going **backwards in time**: a monotonic reads violation caused by hopping between replicas with different lag.

- Replica R1 is at log position 1,000 (12 comments), R2 at 940 (9 comments).
- Round-robin alternates R1, R2, R1.

Pinning the user to one replica means each read sees a position ≥ the last. If that replica fails, rehash to another, and carry the last-seen position so the new replica waits until it's caught up.

questions.prompt: Which of these genuinely need **linearizability** (not just eventual or causal consistency)? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ensuring two people can't register the same username
options.explanation: Correct. Both registration attempts must see one agreed state; with weaker models, two replicas could each accept 'alice'.

options.text: Choosing which node is the current leader
options.explanation: Correct. All nodes must agree on a single leader; disagreement leads to split brain.

options.text: Counting likes on a post
options.explanation: Wrong. Showing 1,203 instead of 1,205 briefly is harmless; a CRDT counter with eventual consistency is ideal.

options.text: Displaying replies after the posts they reply to
options.explanation: Wrong. That needs causal consistency, which is weaker and remains available during partitions.

options.text: Preventing an account balance going below zero across concurrent withdrawals
options.explanation: Correct. Each withdrawal must see the effect of all previous ones; otherwise two concurrent withdrawals can both pass the balance check.

questions.workedExample:
Ask: "does correctness need everyone to agree on the *latest* value right now?"

- Username uniqueness: yes, it's a compare-and-set on one value.
- Leader: yes, it's a lock.
- Balance check: yes, it's a constraint over the latest value.
- Likes: no, approximate is fine.
- Reply order: only causal order matters.

Keeping the linearizable core small is how systems stay fast.

questions.prompt: What does **eventual consistency** guarantee?

options.text: Reads return the latest write within a bounded time, e.g. 1 second.
options.explanation: Wrong. Eventual consistency gives no time bound at all; bounded staleness is a separate, stronger model.

options.text: Clients see their own writes immediately.
options.explanation: Wrong. That's read-your-writes, an extra session guarantee that plain eventual consistency doesn't include.

options.text: All clients see writes in the same order.
options.explanation: Wrong. Agreement on order is part of sequential consistency and stronger; eventual consistency allows replicas to apply writes in different orders as long as they converge.

options.text: If writes stop, all replicas will eventually converge to the same value.
options.explanation: Correct. That's the whole promise: convergence in the absence of new writes. Interim reads can be stale or out of order.

questions.workedExample:
Strip it to the definition: **liveness only**. Eventually, with no new updates, replicas agree.

It says nothing about:

- how long (could be ms or hours),
- what you read meanwhile,
- the order writes appear in.

And to converge, replicas need a deterministic conflict rule (LWW, CRDT merge). That's why people add session guarantees on top.

questions.prompt: A system offers **serializable** transactions but not linearizability. Alice commits a transaction setting her balance to £50 (from £100). One second later, in real time, she runs a read-only transaction and sees £100. Is that allowed?

options.text: No: serializability forbids reading stale data.
options.explanation: Wrong. Serializability only requires equivalence to *some* serial order; ordering the read before the write is a valid serial order, even though it contradicts real time.

options.text: Yes: serializability doesn't require the serial order to respect real time.
options.explanation: Correct. Placing the read-only transaction before the write gives a valid serial history. Forbidding this needs strict serializability (serializable + linearizable).

options.text: Yes, but only if the two transactions touched different rows.
options.explanation: Wrong. They touch the same row; the anomaly is allowed regardless, because serializability ignores real-time ordering.

options.text: No: any serializable database is automatically linearizable.
options.explanation: Wrong. They're independent properties. Serializability is about multi-object transactions; linearizability is about real-time recency. A system can have one without the other.

questions.workedExample:
1. Serial orders available: [T_write, T_read] or [T_read, T_write].
2. [T_read, T_write] produces read = £100, write = £50. Valid serial execution.
3. Serializability is satisfied.
4. But T_read started after T_write committed, so linearizability (real time) is violated.

This happens in practice with snapshot reads on lagging replicas. Spanner's TrueTime commit-wait exists precisely to rule this out, giving **strict serializability**.

questions.prompt: Your global social app must keep working in every region during a trans-Atlantic partition, and must never show a reply before the post it answers. Clients remain with their region during the partition and dependencies are tracked. Which listed model best fits?

options.text: Linearizability
options.explanation: Wrong. Linearizability can't stay available on both sides of a partition (CAP); one side would have to reject requests.

options.text: Sequential consistency
options.explanation: Wrong. Sequential consistency also needs a single global order agreed by all nodes, which a partitioned system can't maintain while both sides accept writes.

options.text: Causal consistency
options.explanation: Correct under the stated sticky-client assumption. Causal dependencies keep replies behind their posts, while each region can continue local work. Moving a client to a replica missing its dependencies can require waiting.

options.text: Eventual consistency only
options.explanation: Wrong. Eventual consistency stays available, but it doesn't guarantee reply-after-post ordering. You can do better.

questions.workedExample:
Two requirements:

1. **Available during partitions** rules out linearizable and sequential (both need global agreement on order).
2. **Reply after post** is a causal dependency: the reply was written after reading the post.

Causal consistency tracks dependencies (e.g. reply carries 'depends on post #123 @ version vector V'). A replica only exposes the reply once it has the post. Each side of the partition keeps working; histories merge after healing.

The availability claim assumes clients remain with a replica that has their causal history. Arbitrary migration during a partition is not covered.

questions.prompt: Client A writes x = 1 and gets an acknowledgement. A second later (in real time), client B, which has never communicated with A, reads x and gets **0**, the initial value. Which consistency models permit this history? Select all that apply.

options.text: Linearizability
options.explanation: Not permitted. B's read started after A's write completed in real time, so it must return 1 or something newer.

options.text: Sequential consistency
options.explanation: Permitted. The total order "B reads 0, then A writes 1" respects each client's own program order. Sequential consistency doesn't require the order to match real time across clients.

options.text: Causal consistency
options.explanation: Permitted. A's write and B's read are not causally related (B never saw anything from A), so B may observe the older state.

options.text: Eventual consistency
options.explanation: Permitted. Eventual consistency allows stale reads in the meantime; it only promises convergence once writes stop.

questions.workedExample:
Check each model's rule against the history:

```
A: |--w x=1--|
B:              |--r x--| -> 0
```

1. **Linearizable**: real-time order is binding. The write finished before the read began, so the read must see it. ✗
2. **Sequential**: find *any* single order that respects each client's program order. [B: read 0, A: write 1] works. ✓
3. **Causal**: only causally related operations must be ordered. There's no path from A's write to B's read. ✓
4. **Eventual**: anything goes in the interim. ✓

The moment B learns about A's write through some other channel (A phones B), real time starts to matter, and only linearizability protects you.

questions.prompt: Your app gives read-your-writes by having the client keep the log position (LSN) of its last write and sending it with each read. A user edits their profile on their **phone**, then opens the **laptop** app and sees the old profile. What is the best fix?

options.text: Make all replicas synchronous.
options.explanation: Wrong. It would work, but it makes every write wait for every replica and fail when any replica is down. That's a heavy price for a per-user guarantee.

options.text: Clear the laptop's cache on start-up.
options.explanation: Wrong. The stale data comes from a lagging replica, not the laptop's cache. A fresh read can still hit the same lagging replica.

options.text: Record the user's last-write LSN on the server side (per user), so any device's read is served only by a replica that has caught up to it.
options.explanation: Correct. The token lived only on the phone. Storing it per user, where every device can use it, extends read-your-writes across devices without global coordination.

options.text: Switch to eventual consistency.
options.explanation: Wrong. That is already the underlying behaviour; it's what causes the anomaly.

questions.workedExample:
Why it failed:

1. Phone writes at LSN 5,000 and remembers 5,000 locally.
2. Laptop has no token, so its read goes to any replica.
3. A replica at LSN 4,950 answers with the old profile.

Fix: keep `last_write_lsn` per **user** (for example in the session store or a small table keyed by user id). Each read looks it up and goes to a replica at or past that LSN, or to the leader. A simpler, coarser alternative: route a user's reads to the leader for a minute after any write by that user.

questions.prompt: A sharded database guarantees **serializable** transactions. T1 credits £100 to account X (shard 1) and commits. Afterwards, in real time, T2 credits £50 to account Y (shard 2). An auditor's read-only T3 sees Y's credit but **not** X's. Which guarantee would rule this out?

options.text: None is needed: serializability already forbids it.
options.explanation: Wrong. The serial order T2, T3, T1 explains exactly what T3 saw, so the history is serializable. It just contradicts real time.

options.text: Strict serializability
options.explanation: Correct. Strict serializability requires the serial order to respect real time. T1 committed before T2 started, so T1 must come first, and any transaction that sees T2 must also see T1.

options.text: Read-your-writes
options.explanation: Wrong. That's a per-session guarantee about a client seeing its own writes. The auditor wrote nothing.

options.text: Snapshot isolation
options.explanation: Wrong. Snapshot isolation is weaker than serializability and also doesn't require snapshots to respect real-time order across shards.

questions.workedExample:
Look for a serial order that explains T3:

1. T3 sees T2 but not T1.
2. Order [T2, T3, T1] produces exactly that. So it's **serializable**.
3. But in real time T1 finished before T2 began. A real-time-respecting order must have T1 before T2, and then T3 couldn't see T2 without T1.
4. So it violates **strict serializability**.

This "causal reverse" anomaly is possible when shards assign commit timestamps from unsynchronised clocks. Spanner rules it out with TrueTime and commit wait.

questions.prompt: Which statements about consistency models are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every linearizable history is also sequentially consistent.
options.explanation: True. The linearization order is a single total order that respects real time, so it also respects each client's program order.

options.text: If every key is linearizable on its own, operations across all keys together are linearizable.
options.explanation: True. Linearizability is local (composable), which is why you can shard keys across independent linearizable groups.

options.text: A serializable database is automatically linearizable.
options.explanation: False. Serializability allows a serial order that contradicts real time, for example a read-only transaction ordered before a write that finished earlier.

options.text: Sequential consistency requires operations from different clients to appear in real-time order.
options.explanation: False. It only requires one total order that respects each client's own program order. Respecting real time across clients is what linearizability adds.

options.text: Strict serializability means serializable plus real-time ordering of transactions.
options.explanation: True. It's the transactional analogue of linearizability, sometimes called external consistency.

questions.workedExample:
Sort the models by two features:

| Model | Transactions? | Real time? |
|---|---|---|
| Linearizable | no | yes |
| Sequential | no | no |
| Serializable | yes | no |
| Strict serializable | yes | yes |

- Linearizable ⇒ sequential: yes, real time is stricter than per-client order.
- Composability: a property of linearizability, not of sequential consistency.
- Serializable ⇒ linearizable: no, the real-time column differs.

questions.prompt: Bob posts "A" and Carol posts "B" at about the same time; neither has seen the other's post. Dave's first read of the feed shows only A. Erin's first read shows only B. What is the **strongest** model this history is consistent with?

options.text: Linearizability
options.explanation: Wrong. One copy of the feed would contain A and B in a single order, so it couldn't show A without B to one reader and B without A to another.

options.text: Sequential consistency
options.explanation: Wrong. Sequential consistency needs one total order of the two writes that every reader agrees on. If A comes first, nobody can see B without A, yet Erin did.

options.text: Causal consistency
options.explanation: Correct. The two posts are concurrent (neither caused the other), and causal consistency lets different readers see concurrent writes in different orders.

options.text: Only eventual consistency
options.explanation: Wrong. The history is causally consistent too, and causal is stronger than eventual.

questions.workedExample:
1. Is there a causal link between the posts? Neither author saw the other's, so no: they are **concurrent**.
2. Sequential: pick an order. [A, B] means Erin's read of "B only" is impossible; [B, A] means Dave's "A only" is impossible. ✗
3. Causal: only causally related writes must be ordered. Concurrent ones may appear in any order to different readers. ✓

If Carol had replied to Bob's post, the reply would be causally after A, and causal consistency would forbid anyone seeing the reply without A.

lessons.title: Time and ordering
lessons.summary: Why wall clocks lie, how NTP works, and how Lamport clocks, vector clocks, hybrid logical clocks and TrueTime order events.
lessons.body:
Many distributed problems boil down to "which happened first?". Which write wins? Did this message cause that one? Is this lease still valid? On one machine the answer comes from a single clock. Across machines there is no shared clock, so you need to be careful about what "first" even means.

## Physical clocks and their problems

Each server has two kinds of clock:

| Clock | Use | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Time-of-day | Timestamps | Can jump back or forward |
| Monotonic | Measuring durations | Only moves forward |

In Linux these are `CLOCK_REALTIME` and `CLOCK_MONOTONIC`. Rule one: **never measure a timeout with the time-of-day clock**. An NTP step can make an elapsed time negative.

### Drift and skew

Quartz crystals run slightly fast or slow, and it varies with temperature. Typical drift is 10 to 200 parts per million.

- 200 ppm × 86,400 s = **17 s per day** if never corrected.
- **Skew** is the difference between two clocks at one moment.

### NTP

The Network Time Protocol syncs a client with servers arranged in strata (stratum 0 is an atomic clock or GPS; stratum 1 servers attach to it, and so on). A client estimates offset from a round trip:

```
client            server
 t0 |--request--->|
    |             | t1 (receive)
    |             | t2 (send)
 t3 |<--reply-----|

delay  = (t3 - t0) - (t2 - t1)
offset = ((t1 - t0) + (t2 - t3)) / 2
```

The offset formula assumes the network delay is **symmetric**. If the outbound path is slow and the return fast, the estimate is wrong by half the asymmetry. Typical accuracy: around 1 ms on a good LAN, tens of ms over the internet, and much worse under congestion. AWS and Google offer leap-smeared, GPS-backed time services that do better (sub-millisecond, with bounds).

NTP corrects a clock by **slewing** (running it slightly fast or slow) for small offsets and **stepping** (jumping) for large ones. Steps are what make clocks go backwards.

> [!warning] Last-write-wins with skewed clocks
> Node A's clock is 100 ms fast. A client writes v1 on A at A-time 10.100 (real 10.000). 50 ms later a client writes v2 on B at B-time 10.050 (real 10.050). LWW keeps v1 because 10.100 > 10.050, silently discarding the genuinely later write. This is a well-known hazard in Cassandra and other last-write-wins stores: any two writes closer together than the clock skew can be ordered wrongly.

## Happens-before

Lamport's 1978 paper defined order without clocks. Event *a* **happens before** *b* (written a → b) if:

1. a and b are on the same process and a comes first, or
2. a is sending a message and b is receiving that message, or
3. there's an event c with a → c and c → b (transitivity).

If neither a → b nor b → a, the events are **concurrent** (a ∥ b). Concurrent doesn't mean simultaneous; it means neither could have influenced the other.

## Lamport clocks

Each process keeps an integer counter `L`.

- Before every local event or send: `L = L + 1`; attach `L` to sends.
- On receive with timestamp `t`: `L = max(L, t) + 1`.

```
 P1        P2        P3
 1 a
 2 send--->3 recv
           4 b
           5 send--->6 recv
 3 c                 7 d
```

Guarantee: if a → b then L(a) < L(b). Break ties with process id to get a **total order** consistent with causality. That's enough for things like a totally ordered mutex queue.

Limitation: the converse fails. L(c)=3 < L(b)=4 but c and b are concurrent. **A Lamport timestamp can't tell you whether two events are concurrent.**

Read the guarantee the right way round:

- L(a) < L(b): a *might* have happened before b, or they might be concurrent.
- L(a) = L(b) on different processes: they are **definitely concurrent**, because causally related events always have different timestamps.
- L(a) > L(b): a did **not** happen before b. Either b happened before a, or they're concurrent.

### Logical clocks you already use

Many systems contain a Lamport-style counter under another name: Raft's **term**, Paxos's **ballot number**, Kafka's **leader epoch**, ZooKeeper's **zxid**. Each is a number that only goes up and is carried on messages, so a node that sees a higher one knows its own information is out of date. Lesson 6 uses exactly this property for fencing tokens.

## Vector clocks

A vector clock keeps one counter **per process**. For N processes, each holds `V[1..N]`.

- Local event or send: `V[i] += 1`; attach V to sends.
- Receive V': `V[j] = max(V[j], V'[j])` for all j, then `V[i] += 1`.

Compare two vectors:

- V ≤ W if every entry of V ≤ the matching entry of W.
- V → W (happened before) if V ≤ W and V ≠ W.
- If W ≤ V and W ≠ V, W happened before V.
- Distinct events are **concurrent** only when neither vector is component-wise less than or equal to the other.

```
P1: [1,0,0] a
P1: [2,0,0] send to P2
P2: [2,1,0] recv
P2: [2,2,0] send to P3
P3: [0,0,1] e (before recv)
P3: [2,2,2] recv
P1: [3,0,0] c
```

Is c → [2,2,0]? Compare [3,0,0] vs [2,2,0]: 3 > 2 in one position, 0 < 2 in another. **Concurrent.** Vector clocks can detect that, which is why Dynamo and Riak used them to keep both sibling values instead of silently dropping one.

Cost: one entry per participant. With thousands of clients as writers, vectors bloat, so systems use **version vectors** keyed by replica (not client), or prune old entries (at the risk of false conflicts).

## Hybrid logical clocks (HLC)

HLC (Kulkarni et al., 2014) combines physical time with a logical counter. Each timestamp is a pair `(l, c)`:

- `l` tracks the largest physical time seen,
- `c` is a counter that breaks ties when `l` doesn't advance.

Rules on a send or local event, with physical time `pt`:

```
l' = max(l, pt)
if l' == l: c = c + 1
else:       c = 0
l = l'
```

On receive of `(lm, cm)`, take the max of `l`, `lm` and `pt`, and set c accordingly (incrementing from whichever input matched).

Properties:

- Respects happens-before like a Lamport clock (and, like one, can't detect concurrency).
- Stays within the clock-skew bound ε of real time, so timestamps are human-meaningful.
- Can use compact fixed-size encodings; exact timestamp widths depend on the implementation.

CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use HLCs for MVCC timestamps. CockroachDB adds a **maximum clock offset** (500 ms by default) and an "uncertainty interval": if a read sees a value whose timestamp is within that window above the read timestamp, it can't tell whether it happened before the read, so it restarts the read at a higher timestamp. A node that detects its clock is too far from the rest of the cluster shuts itself down rather than risk violating the bound.

## TrueTime and Spanner

Google Spanner takes the opposite approach: make physical time trustworthy by **bounding the uncertainty**. Each data centre has GPS receivers and atomic clocks. The TrueTime API returns an interval:

```
TT.now() -> [earliest, latest]
error bound ε: 1-7 ms in the 2012 paper
```

Real time is guaranteed to be inside the interval, which is about 2ε wide. ε isn't fixed: it grows between synchronisations with the time masters (to allow for local drift) and shrinks after each one. If the time masters become unreachable, ε keeps growing, and Spanner gets **slower** (longer commit waits) rather than incorrect.

### Commit wait

To commit a transaction, Spanner:

1. picks timestamp `s = TT.now().latest`,
2. waits until `TT.now().earliest > s`,
3. then makes the commit visible.

```
     s = latest
       |
 [--ε--|--ε--]
       |<-wait->|
                commit visible
```

After the wait, `s` is definitely in the past on every clock. Any transaction that starts later in real time will get a larger timestamp. That's how Spanner gets **external consistency** (strict serializability) with timestamp ordering, at the cost of waiting about 2ε per commit, typically a few milliseconds.

> [!tip] The trade-off in one line
> Spanner spends money on hardware to make ε small, then waits it out. CockroachDB, on commodity clocks with bigger ε, avoids waiting on writes but sometimes restarts reads instead.

## Summary comparison

| Clock | Detects concurrency? | Size |
|---|---|---|
| Physical (NTP) | No, and can be wrong | 64 bits |
| Lamport | No | 1 integer |
| Vector | Yes | N integers |
| HLC | No | Implementation-dependent |
| TrueTime | Bounded interval | 2 timestamps |

## Key takeaways
- Use monotonic clocks for durations; time-of-day clocks drift, get stepped by NTP and can go backwards.
- NTP gives roughly millisecond accuracy on a LAN and assumes symmetric delay; skew makes last-write-wins lose data.
- Happens-before is defined by process order and messages; events with no such path are concurrent.
- Lamport clocks give a total order consistent with causality but can't detect concurrency; vector clocks can, at O(N) size.
- Hybrid logical clocks combine physical time and counters; CockroachDB uses them with an uncertainty interval.
- Spanner's TrueTime bounds clock error and uses commit wait to achieve external consistency.
