lessons.title: Leader election, leases and distributed locks
lessons.summary: Why every distributed lock is really a lease, how fencing tokens stop stale holders doing damage, and the Redlock debate.
lessons.body:
Many systems need exactly one actor doing something at a time: one scheduler running cron jobs, one primary database, one worker processing a given file. On a single machine you'd take a mutex. Across machines, it's much harder, because the holder can crash, pause or be cut off while holding it.

## Locks are really leases

A distributed lock that never expires is useless: if the holder crashes, nobody can ever take it. So every practical distributed lock has a timeout. A lock with a timeout is a **lease**: "you own this for the next 10 seconds, renew it if you want to keep it."

```
client A        lock service
  |--acquire----->|  lease 10 s
  |<--granted-----|
  |  ... work ... |
  |--renew------->|  every ~3 s
  |<--ok----------|
```

The holder renews well before expiry (often at a third of the lease). If it crashes, renewals stop and the lease expires, letting someone else take over.

### Why use a lease for leader election?

Leader election is a lock on the role "leader". Kubernetes controllers use a `Lease` object (in the `coordination.k8s.io` API, stored in etcd behind the API server); HDFS and HBase use ZooKeeper ephemeral nodes; AWS describes the same pattern with DynamoDB conditional writes in its Builders' Library.

Choosing the lease duration is a trade-off:

| Lease | Pro | Con |
|---|---|---|
| Short (2 s) | Fast failover | False expiry on GC/network blips |
| Long (60 s) | Few false failovers | Long outage if holder dies |

## The fundamental problem: the holder doesn't know it lost

A lease expiry is decided by the lock service's clock. The holder only *believes* it holds the lease, based on its own sense of time. Process pauses break that belief:

```
A            lock svc        storage
|--acquire-->|
|<--ok, 10s--|
| GC pause...
|            | lease expires
|            |<--acquire-- B
|            |---ok-------> B
|            |       B writes ->|
| ...resumes |
|--write (thinks it holds)----->|
          CORRUPTION
```

Checking "do I still hold the lease?" right before writing doesn't help: the pause can happen *between* the check and the write. Network delays do the same: A's write can sit in a TCP buffer and arrive after B's.

> [!warning] You can't fix this on the client
> Any client-side check is a check-then-act race. The only safe place to reject a stale holder is the resource being protected.

### Holder-side hygiene still matters

Client checks can't make a lease *safe*, but they make trouble rarer, and getting them wrong makes it common:

- **Start the clock before you ask.** Record the monotonic time just *before* sending the acquire request, and count the lease from then. The service starts its countdown when it grants, which is later, so the holder's view expires first.
- **Use the monotonic clock**, never the time-of-day clock, so an NTP step can't extend the lease.
- **Leave a margin for clock rate drift.** Two machines don't need synchronised clocks for leases, but their clocks must run at roughly the same *rate*. Stop acting a little before your local expiry.

## Fencing tokens

The fix, described in the Chubby paper and popularised by Martin Kleppmann: every time the lock service grants the lock, it also returns a **fencing token**, a number that strictly increases with each grant.

- The client sends the token with every request to the protected resource.
- The resource remembers the highest token it has seen and **rejects** any request with a lower one.

```
A gets lock, token 33
A pauses
lease expires
B gets lock, token 34
B writes (34)  -> storage: max=34 OK
A wakes, writes (33)
               -> storage: 33<34 REJECT
```

Once the resource has accepted a higher token, it rejects lower-token writes. Acquisition alone does not notify the resource: register the new epoch before reading or acting on state when the protocol requires that boundary.

### Where tokens come from

| System | Natural fencing token |
|---|---|
| etcd | Lock key's `create_revision` or `mod_revision` |
| ZooKeeper | `zxid` or znode `cversion`/sequence number |
| Raft/Paxos | The term or ballot number |
| Database | A version column updated with each grant |

Raft's **term** is itself a fencing token: followers reject `AppendEntries` from a leader with a lower term. That's why stale Raft leaders can't corrupt the log.

### The catch

The resource has to cooperate. A database can do it with a conditional update:

```
UPDATE jobs
SET owner = 'B', token = 34
WHERE id = 7 AND token <= 34;
```

The `<=` lets the current holder write repeatedly with the same token, while any lower (stale) token matches no rows. Check the affected row count: zero means you've been fenced off.

The check must also happen in **one consistent place**. If the "resource" is three asynchronously replicated copies that each track their own highest token, a stale write can still succeed on a copy that hasn't yet seen the newer token. A single leader or a linearizable conditional write does the job; independent replicas don't.

An S3 bucket, a payment API or an email server generally won't check your token. For those, you need idempotency (so a duplicate is harmless) or you must accept the risk.

## Efficiency locks versus correctness locks

Kleppmann distinguishes two purposes:

- **Efficiency**: avoid doing the same work twice (e.g. two workers both regenerating a report). An occasional double run wastes money but is harmless.
- **Correctness**: two holders would corrupt data, double-charge or lose updates.

For efficiency, a simple single-node Redis lock (`SET key token NX PX 10000`) is perfectly fine. For correctness, you need a consensus-backed lock service *and* fencing at the resource.

Even an efficiency lock needs a careful **release**. A plain `DEL key` is wrong: if your lease expired during a pause and someone else acquired the lock, you'd delete *their* lock. Release only if the value is still your random token, atomically, with a small Lua script:

```
if redis.call("get", KEYS[1])
   == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("del", KEYS[1])
end
return 0
```

## Redlock and why it's controversial

Redlock is an algorithm proposed by Salvatore Sanfilippo (antirez), Redis's creator, for a lock that survives a Redis node failing. It uses N independent Redis masters (typically 5), with no replication between them:

1. Get the current time T1.
2. Try `SET resource token NX PX ttl` on all 5 instances, with a short per-node timeout.
3. Get the time T2. The lock is held if a majority (≥ 3) succeeded **and** T2 − T1 < ttl.
4. The validity time is ttl − (T2 − T1) − clock drift allowance.
5. On failure, release on all instances.

### Kleppmann's critique (2016)

1. **No fencing tokens.** Redlock returns a random value, not a monotonically increasing number, so a resource can't tell an old holder from a new one. Process pauses still cause two holders, as in the diagram above.
2. **It depends on timing assumptions.** Safety relies on bounded network delay, bounded pauses and clocks that don't jump. If a Redis node's clock jumps forward (NTP step, admin change), its key expires early:

```
C1 locks A, B, C   (3 of 5)
C's clock jumps forward
  -> C expires C1's key
C2 locks C, D, E   (3 of 5)
Both C1 and C2 think they hold it
```

A node crashing and restarting without persisted keys (or with `fsync` every second) has the same effect.

His conclusion: Redlock is too heavy for efficiency locks (one Redis is fine) and not safe enough for correctness locks (use ZooKeeper or etcd with fencing).

### Antirez's response

Antirez argued that:

- the random token can be used for compare-and-set at the resource in some cases;
- Redlock's step 3 detects long delays *during acquisition*;
- clock jumps can be avoided operationally by slewing rather than stepping, so the timing assumptions are reasonable;
- every lock with auto-release has the GC pause problem, including ZooKeeper's.

The last point is true, and it's exactly why fencing tokens are the real answer: they make safety independent of timing. Redlock's problem is that it doesn't produce one.

> [!tip] Practical guidance
> For efficiency only, a single Redis `SET NX PX` is fine. For correctness, use etcd, ZooKeeper or Consul, *plus* fencing tokens at the resource, *plus* idempotency where the resource can't check tokens. Or partition work by key, as Kafka consumer groups do, and enforce sequencing or fencing at external storage so a stale consumer cannot reorder writes during a rebalance.

## Key takeaways
- Any distributed lock that can auto-expire is a lease; holders must renew, and lease length trades failover speed against false expiry.
- A holder can't reliably know it has lost the lease, because pauses and delays can strike between check and act.
- Fencing tokens (monotonically increasing per grant) let the protected resource reject stale holders, making safety independent of timing. The check must happen in one consistent place.
- Holders should time leases from before the request, on the monotonic clock, and release locks only if they still own them.
- etcd revisions, ZooKeeper zxids and Raft terms all serve as fencing tokens.
- Distinguish efficiency locks (single Redis is fine) from correctness locks (consensus plus fencing).
- Redlock lacks fencing tokens and relies on bounded clocks and pauses, which is why Kleppmann argued it is unsafe for correctness.

## Further reading
- [How to do distributed locking (Martin Kleppmann)](https://martin.kleppmann.com/2016/02/08/how-to-do-distributed-locking.html)
- [Is Redlock safe? (antirez's reply)](http://antirez.com/news/101)
- [Distributed locks with Redis (Redis docs)](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/use/patterns/distributed-locks/)
- [Leader election in distributed systems (AWS Builders' Library)](https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/leader-election-in-distributed-systems/)
- [ZooKeeper recipes: locks and leader election](https://zookeeper.apache.org/doc/current/recipes.html)
- [Leases (Kubernetes docs)](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/)

questions.prompt: Why do practical distributed locks always have an expiry time?

options.text: To save memory in the lock service.
options.explanation: Wrong. A lock entry is a few bytes; memory isn't the reason.

options.text: Because the network forces TCP connections to close.
options.explanation: Wrong. Lock lifetimes aren't tied to TCP connections in general; and if they were, a stuck but connected holder would block forever.

options.text: So that a crashed holder doesn't block everyone forever.
options.explanation: Correct. The lock service can't tell whether the holder is dead or just quiet, so it must release the lock eventually, which makes it a lease.

options.text: To guarantee only one holder at a time.
options.explanation: Wrong, in fact the opposite: expiry is what *allows* two holders when the old one is merely paused. Safety needs fencing tokens.

questions.workedExample:
1. Without expiry: holder crashes → lock held forever → system stuck.
2. With expiry: holder must renew; if it crashes, renewals stop; after the TTL someone else can acquire.
3. Side effect: a holder that's paused (not dead) also stops renewing and loses the lock without noticing. That's why expiry alone can't guarantee mutual exclusion.

questions.prompt: Worker A holds a lock with fencing token 41 and pauses. The lease expires. Worker B acquires token 42 and writes. Then B releases and C acquires 43 but hasn't written yet. A wakes and writes with token 41. What does a storage service that enforces fencing do?

options.text: Rejects it, because 41 < 42, the highest token it has seen.
options.explanation: Correct. Storage tracks the max token from any accepted request. B's write recorded 42, so A's 41 is stale and rejected.

options.text: Accepts it, because C hasn't written yet so the highest seen is still 41.
options.explanation: Wrong. Storage has already seen 42 from B's write, so the highest seen is 42.

options.text: Accepts it, because 41 was a valid token when issued.
options.explanation: Wrong. Validity at issue time is irrelevant; the whole point is rejecting tokens that have since been superseded.

options.text: Asks the lock service whether A still holds the lock.
options.explanation: Wrong. That's another check-then-act race and adds a dependency; fencing works by comparing numbers locally at the resource.

questions.workedExample:
Storage state over time:

| Event | max token |
|---|---|
| start | 40 |
| B writes (42) | 42 |
| C acquires 43 (no write) | 42 |
| A writes (41) | 41 < 42 → **reject** |

Note that storage only learns about tokens from requests it receives. That's fine: any token lower than one already used is definitely stale.

questions.prompt: A nightly job regenerates a cached report. If two instances run at once, the only harm is wasted CPU. Which lock is appropriate?

options.text: Redlock across 5 Redis masters
options.explanation: Wrong. More complex and expensive than needed; for an efficiency lock its extra fault tolerance buys little.

options.text: ZooKeeper lock with fencing tokens enforced at the cache
options.explanation: Wrong. Correct but over-engineered; fencing matters when a double holder causes damage, which isn't the case here.

options.text: No lock at all, ever
options.explanation: Wrong. Some coordination is cheap and avoids burning CPU every night on duplicate work; 'no lock' isn't the best answer here.

options.text: A single Redis `SET key value NX PX 60000`
options.explanation: Correct. This is an efficiency lock: an occasional double run after a Redis failover is harmless, so a single node is simple and good enough.

questions.workedExample:
Classify the lock:

1. What happens with two holders? Duplicate computation, same result.
2. That's an **efficiency** lock.
3. Pick the cheapest mechanism that usually prevents duplicates: single-node Redis with NX (only set if absent) and PX (expiry).
4. Release with a compare-and-delete (Lua script checking the random value) so you don't delete someone else's lock.

questions.prompt: Which are valid criticisms of using Redlock for a **correctness** lock? Select all that apply.

options.text: It doesn't generate monotonically increasing fencing tokens.
options.explanation: Correct. Its random values can't be ordered, so a resource can't reject a stale holder by comparing numbers.

options.text: A clock jump on one Redis node can expire a key early, letting a second client get a majority.
options.explanation: Correct. Redlock's safety relies on TTLs measured by each node's clock; a forward jump on one of the majority nodes breaks mutual exclusion.

options.text: Redis is too slow to acquire locks quickly.
options.explanation: Wrong. Redis is extremely fast; speed isn't the concern.

options.text: A node that restarts without persisting keys can forget a lock and grant it again.
options.explanation: Correct. Without fsync on every write, a crash-restart loses the key, and a second client can then reach a majority.

options.text: It needs at least 7 Redis nodes to be safe.
options.explanation: Wrong. The node count isn't the issue; Redlock with 5 nodes tolerates 2 failures by design. The problems are timing assumptions and missing fencing.

questions.workedExample:
Kleppmann's argument had two parts:

1. **No fencing**: even a perfect lock service can't stop a paused ex-holder unless the resource checks an increasing token. Redlock gives random strings.
2. **Timing assumptions**: safety depends on bounded clock drift, network delay and pauses. Examples that break it:
  - clock jump on node C → C1's key expires early → C2 gets C, D, E;
  - node C crash-restart without fsync → same effect.

Performance and node count aren't the issue.

questions.prompt: A Kubernetes-style controller uses a 15-second lease in etcd and renews every 5 seconds. Its process suffers a 20-second GC pause right after a successful renewal. Another replica takes over at t = 15 s. The protected records are in that same etcd cluster. What is the safest design for its writes?

options.text: Check `time.now() < lease_expiry` before each write.
options.explanation: Wrong. The pause can happen between the check and the write; the check passes, the write lands after expiry.

options.text: Include the lease's etcd revision in each write as a transaction condition, so writes from an old lease holder fail.
options.explanation: Correct for writes in the same etcd transaction. Compare the leadership key revision and update the protected keys atomically. A separate check followed by an external write would still race.

options.text: Make the lease 30 seconds so 20-second pauses are covered.
options.explanation: Wrong. Pauses are unbounded; a 35-second pause breaks it, and failover becomes slower for every real crash.

options.text: Disable garbage collection on the controller.
options.explanation: Wrong. Pauses also come from VM migration, swapping and network delay; removing GC doesn't remove the problem.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline:

```
t=0   renew; lease to t=15
t=0   GC pause begins
t=15  lease expires
t=15  replica 2 becomes leader
t=20  replica 1 resumes, writes
```

Fixes ranked:

1. Client-side time checks: race, unsafe.
2. Longer lease: makes the window rarer, not impossible.
3. **Fencing**: `Txn(If(mod_revision(leader_key) == my_rev)).Then(put ...)` fails for replica 1 because replica 2's election changed the revision. Safe whatever the timing.

questions.prompt: You choose a lease of **2 seconds** for your database primary election instead of 30 seconds. What's the main new risk?

options.text: Frequent false failovers from brief GC pauses or network blips.
options.explanation: Correct. Any hiccup over ~2 s causes the lease to lapse and a new election, which means disruption, possible data loss on async replicas and churn.

options.text: Slower failover when the primary crashes.
options.explanation: Wrong. Shorter leases mean *faster* failover; that's their main benefit.

options.text: The lock service will run out of leases.
options.explanation: Wrong. Lease count is unaffected by duration.

options.text: Two primaries become impossible.
options.explanation: Wrong. Lease length doesn't make split brain impossible; only fencing does. Shorter leases make false expiry more likely, not less.

questions.workedExample:
Trade-off:

| Lease | Detection on real crash | False expiry risk |
|---|---|---|
| 2 s | ~2 s | high |
| 30 s | ~30 s | low |

A 2 s lease with renewal every ~0.7 s fails if any renewal path stalls for over ~1.3 s: a GC pause, a busy etcd, a slow disk fsync. Each false failover may lose unreplicated writes and restart connections, so many teams settle around 10–15 s.

questions.prompt: Your lock protects calls to a third-party payment API that has no notion of fencing tokens. Two holders could double-charge. What's the best mitigation?

options.text: Use Redlock with 7 nodes instead of 5.
options.explanation: Wrong. More nodes don't fix pauses or missing fencing; a stale holder can still call the API.

options.text: Rely on etcd's linearizability.
options.explanation: Wrong. etcd guarantees agreement on who holds the lock, but can't stop a paused ex-holder's in-flight call reaching the external API.

options.text: Send an idempotency key derived from the operation (e.g. order id) so repeated calls have no extra effect.
options.explanation: Correct. When the resource can't check tokens, making the operation idempotent means a stale holder's duplicate call is harmless.

options.text: Shorten the lease to 1 second.
options.explanation: Wrong. Shorter leases increase false expiry and do nothing about stale holders; they make it worse.

questions.workedExample:
1. Fencing needs the resource to compare tokens; the payment API won't.
2. So the lock alone can't give safety.
3. Move safety to the operation: an idempotency key like `charge:order-9182` means the processor returns the original result on a duplicate instead of charging again.
4. Stripe, Adyen and most payment APIs support this.

Rule: lock for efficiency, idempotency (or fencing) for correctness.

questions.prompt: A client acquires a 10-second lease. The request takes 300 ms to reach the lock service and the reply 300 ms to come back. From which moment should the **client** count its 10 seconds?

options.text: From the moment it receives the reply, since that's when it knows it holds the lease.
options.explanation: Wrong. The service started counting when it granted, about 300 ms before the reply arrived. Counting from receipt makes the client think it holds the lease ~300 ms longer than it does.

options.text: From the timestamp in the reply, converted from the service's wall clock.
options.explanation: Wrong. That compares wall clocks across two machines, which are skewed and can jump. The client should rely only on its own monotonic clock.

options.text: It doesn't matter, because 300 ms is small compared with 10 s.
options.explanation: Wrong. Delays can be far larger than 300 ms under load, and the error is always in the unsafe direction.

options.text: From just before it sent the request, measured on its monotonic clock, minus a safety margin.
options.explanation: Correct. The grant can't have happened before the request was sent, so counting from then guarantees the client's view of expiry comes no later than the service's, as long as clock rates are similar.

questions.workedExample:
Timeline on a common scale:

```
t=0.0  client sends (start here)
t=0.3  service grants; expires 10.3
t=0.6  client gets reply
```

- Count from 0.0: client stops at 10.0 (minus margin), before 10.3. Safe side.
- Count from 0.6: client acts until 10.6, after expiry. Unsafe.

This narrows the danger window but doesn't remove it: a pause can still strike between "lease still valid" and the write. That's what fencing tokens are for.

questions.prompt: Which of these can serve as a **fencing token**, one that the protected resource can compare to reject a stale lock holder? Select all that apply.

options.text: The etcd revision at which the lock key was created
options.explanation: Correct. etcd revisions are cluster-wide and strictly increasing, so every new acquisition gets a larger number.

options.text: The sequence number of a ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential lock node
options.explanation: Correct. ZooKeeper assigns increasing sequence numbers under a parent, so a later lock holder's node has a higher number.

options.text: The random value Redlock stores in the key
options.explanation: Wrong. Random values can show "this isn't my lock", but can't be ordered, so the resource can't tell whether a request comes from an older or newer holder.

options.text: The lock holder's wall-clock time when it acquired the lock
options.explanation: Wrong. Wall clocks on different machines are skewed and can jump backwards, so a later holder may present a smaller timestamp.

options.text: The Raft term of the leader that issues the writes
options.explanation: Correct. Terms strictly increase with each election, and Raft followers already use them to reject a deposed leader.

questions.workedExample:
A fencing token needs one property: **every new grant gets a strictly larger number than every earlier grant**, decided by a single authority.

| Candidate | Strictly increasing? |
|---|---|
| etcd revision | yes |
| ZK sequence number | yes |
| Redlock random value | no (unordered) |
| Holder's wall clock | no (skew, jumps) |
| Raft term | yes |

The consensus-backed ones work because a single replicated log decides the order of grants.

questions.prompt: You add fencing to a storage service that has three replicas with **asynchronous** replication. Writes go to whichever replica is nearest, and each replica independently rejects tokens lower than the highest it has seen. Holder A (token 33) is paused; B gets token 34 and writes to replica R1. A wakes and writes to R2. What happens?

options.text: R2 rejects A, because 34 is the highest token in the system.
options.explanation: Wrong. R2 only knows tokens it has seen itself. If B's write hasn't replicated to R2 yet, R2's highest is still 33 or lower.

options.text: R2 may accept A's stale write, because it hasn't yet seen token 34. Fencing must be checked in one consistent place.
options.explanation: Correct. Independent checks on asynchronously replicated copies re-create the race fencing was meant to remove. The token check and the write must be one atomic step in a linearizable place, such as a single leader or a conditional write.

options.text: The write is rejected because replicas share tokens instantly over gossip.
options.explanation: Wrong. Gossip is eventually consistent; there's always a window in which R2 hasn't heard about 34.

options.text: Both writes are kept, and the token is used to merge them later.
options.explanation: Wrong. The design rejects or accepts writes; it doesn't merge. And even if replication later orders by token, A's write may already have been read and acted on.

questions.workedExample:
```
R1: max=34 (B wrote)
R2: max=33 (not replicated)
A writes 33 to R2 -> 33 >= 33 OK!
```

The stale holder got through because the "highest token seen" isn't a single agreed value. Fixes:

- Route all writes for the resource through a single leader that checks the token.
- Use a linearizable conditional write (`UPDATE ... WHERE token <= 34`, an etcd transaction, a DynamoDB condition expression).

Fencing moves the problem to the resource; the resource must then be strongly consistent about the token.

questions.prompt: Workers use a single-node Redis lock: `SET lock:report <random> NX PX 30000`. When done, each worker runs `DEL lock:report`. Worker A pauses for 40 s mid-job, B acquires the lock, then A finishes and runs `DEL`. What goes wrong?

options.text: Nothing: DEL fails because A no longer owns the key.
options.explanation: Wrong. Redis has no idea who "owns" a key. DEL deletes it unconditionally.

options.text: Redis rejects the DEL because the key has a TTL.
options.explanation: Wrong. Keys with a TTL can be deleted normally.

options.text: A deletes B's lock, so a third worker C can acquire it while B is still running.
options.explanation: Correct. A's lease expired at 30 s and B took the lock. A's blind DEL removes B's key, and now B and C can both run. Release should delete only if the value still equals A's random token, atomically (a Lua script).

options.text: A's DEL extends B's lock by another 30 s.
options.explanation: Wrong. DEL removes the key; it never extends anything.

questions.workedExample:
1. t=0: A sets lock = "a7f". TTL 30 s.
2. t=30: key expires. B sets lock = "c19".
3. t=40: A resumes and runs `DEL lock:report`, deleting **B's** lock.
4. C acquires: B and C now both run.

Safe release, atomically in Lua:

```
if get(key) == my_token:
    del(key)
```

Wrapping it in a Lua script makes the compare and delete a single step. A still overran its lease (that's inherent), but it no longer breaks the next holder's lock.

questions.prompt: A ledger service must apply each account's transactions one at a time, in order. Volume is high and spread across millions of accounts. Which design avoids a per-account distributed lock while staying safe?

options.text: Partition by account id, process sequentially, and atomically enforce both transaction-id deduplication and a per-account sequence or fencing condition in the ledger.
options.explanation: Correct. Kafka partitions provide input order, but an old consumer can overlap a new owner. The ledger must reject duplicate and out-of-order or stale-owner writes atomically; idempotency alone only rejects repeats of the same transaction.

options.text: Take a Redlock lock on the account id for every transaction.
options.explanation: Wrong. It adds a multi-node round trip per transaction and still lacks fencing, so it isn't safe for correctness anyway.

options.text: Let any worker process any transaction and rely on database autocommit.
options.explanation: Wrong. Concurrent workers could apply an account's transactions out of order or interleave read-modify-write cycles and lose updates.

options.text: Use a single worker for all accounts.
options.explanation: Wrong. It's safe but can't keep up with high volume, and it is a single point of failure.

questions.workedExample:
1. Route each account to one partition and process its records sequentially.
2. During rebalancing, an old consumer may still issue writes.
3. In one ledger transaction, check the expected account sequence (or a validated owner epoch), check the unique transaction id, update the balance and advance the sequence.
4. Reject or retry out-of-order work. Deduplication by transaction id alone would still allow two distinct transactions to apply in the wrong order.

lessons.title: Distributed transactions and sagas
lessons.summary: Two-phase commit and why it blocks, three-phase commit's limits, and sagas with orchestration, choreography and compensating actions.
lessons.body:
A transaction on one database is atomic: all of its writes happen or none do. Once a business operation spans several databases or services (charge a card, reserve stock, book a courier), you need a way to keep them consistent. There are two broad answers: **atomic commit protocols** that make many participants behave like one transaction, and **sagas** that give up atomicity in favour of compensation.

## The atomic commit problem

Every participant must reach the same decision, **commit** or **abort**, and commit is only allowed if *every* participant voted yes. That differs from consensus, where a majority suffices: here a single "no" (constraint violation, out of stock) must abort everything.

## Two-phase commit (2PC)

2PC uses a **coordinator** (often the application's transaction manager) and **participants** (databases, queues).

```
Coordinator       P1         P2
 |--prepare------->|          |
 |--prepare------------------>|
 |<--yes-----------|          |
 |<--yes----------------------|
 | log COMMIT                 |
 |--commit-------->|          |
 |--commit------------------->|
 |<--ack-----------|          |
 |<--ack----------------------|
```

### Phase 1: prepare

The coordinator asks each participant "can you commit?". A participant that says **yes** must first write all the transaction's changes and a prepare record durably to disk, and hold its locks. From then on it has **given up the right to abort**: it must commit if told to, even after a crash and restart.

### Phase 2: commit or abort

If every participant voted yes, the coordinator writes **COMMIT** to its own log (this is the **commit point**) and tells everyone. If any voted no or timed out, it writes **ABORT**. The coordinator retries the phase 2 message until every participant acknowledges, forever if necessary.

There are two points of no return: the participant's yes vote and the coordinator's decision log record.

### Recovery: presumed abort

What if the coordinator crashes and, on restart, finds **no** decision record for a transaction? Then it never reached the commit point, so no participant can have been told to commit. It is safe to abort, and the coordinator does so. This convention, **presumed abort**, means the coordinator only needs to force-write COMMIT records; aborts can be logged lazily or not at all.

Participants that crash recover the same way from their own log: no prepare record means they never voted yes and can abort; a prepare record with no outcome means they are in doubt and must ask the coordinator.

### The blocking problem

Suppose a participant has voted yes and the coordinator then crashes before sending the decision.

```
Coordinator     P1           P2
 |<--yes--------|            |
 |<--yes---------------------|
 X crashes
                P1: in doubt
                P2: in doubt
         holding locks...
```

P1 can't commit (maybe P2 voted no). It can't abort (maybe the coordinator logged COMMIT and P2 already committed). Asking P2 doesn't help if P2 is also in doubt. Both must **wait for the coordinator to recover**, holding row locks the whole time. Other transactions touching those rows block too.

This is why 2PC is called a **blocking protocol**: a single coordinator failure can stall participants indefinitely. In practice, operators sometimes resolve in-doubt transactions by hand (Postgres `COMMIT PREPARED` / `ROLLBACK PREPARED`), which risks inconsistency if they guess differently from the coordinator. Postgres disables prepared transactions by default (`max_prepared_transactions = 0`) partly because forgotten ones hold locks and block vacuum.

### Other costs

- At least two round trips and several forced disk writes (`fsync`) per transaction.
- Locks held across a network round trip, which hurts throughput under contention.
- The slowest participant sets the latency.
- **XA** (the cross-vendor 2PC standard) acts as a lowest common denominator; failure handling across heterogeneous systems is notoriously fragile.

> [!note] 2PC on top of consensus
> Spanner and CockroachDB still use 2PC across shards, but each participant and the coordinator are **Raft or Paxos groups**, not single machines. A coordinator "crash" just means its group elects a new leader, which reads the decision from the replicated log. This permits recovery from an individual coordinator failure while its group retains a quorum; losing that quorum or an essential participant can still block progress. CockroachDB's **parallel commits** go further, overlapping the two phases so that a typical distributed transaction commits after a single round of consensus writes.

## Three-phase commit (3PC)

3PC (Skeen, 1981) inserts a **pre-commit** phase so that no participant is ever uncertain while another might have committed:

```
1. canCommit?   -> yes/no
2. preCommit    -> ack
3. doCommit     -> ack
```

After coordinator failure, survivors run a termination protocol that exchanges their states and coordinates a common outcome. A participant that voted yes must not simply abort on its own because its local preCommit message has not arrived; another survivor may already be prepared.

The catch: this reasoning assumes a **synchronous network with bounded delay and perfect failure detection**. Under a partition, a recovery coordinator may be unable to exchange states with all required participants. Treating local timeout alone as authority to commit or abort can produce conflicting decisions; the termination protocol's synchrony and failure assumptions are essential. Because real networks are partially synchronous, 3PC is rarely used. The practical answer is 2PC with a replicated, consensus-backed coordinator.

## Sagas

Microservices usually can't (or shouldn't) hold locks across services for the duration of a business process. A **saga** (Garcia-Molina and Salem, 1987) breaks a long transaction into a sequence of **local transactions**, each committed immediately in its own service. If a later step fails, previously completed steps are undone by **compensating transactions**.

```
T1 order    T2 payment   T3 stock
created --> charged ----> reserve FAILS
                              |
C2 refund <-------------------+
C1 cancel order
```

### Compensating actions

A compensation is a *semantic* undo, not a rollback. A refund is not the same as never having charged: the customer may see two lines on their statement. Some actions can't be compensated at all (an email sent, a parcel shipped), so order steps carefully:

1. **Compensatable** steps first (create order in PENDING, reserve stock).
2. The **pivot** step: the point of no return (charge the card).
3. **Retriable** steps after the pivot, which must eventually succeed (send confirmation email, notify warehouse).

Compensations must themselves be **idempotent** and retried until they succeed; if a refund call times out, you retry it.

### Timeouts make it harder

A step that times out has an **unknown** outcome, exactly as in lesson 1. If the orchestrator gives up on "charge card" and starts compensating, the charge might still happen later: the request could be sitting in a queue. So:

- A compensation must be safe to run even if the forward step **never happened** (refunding an unknown charge is a no-op).
- The service should record the compensation, so a forward request that arrives **after** it is rejected rather than applied. Use a shared saga or step identifier for correlation, with distinct idempotency keys for the forward action and compensation; a durable step state machine must reject late forward work after cancellation.
- Where possible, ask the service for the step's status (by idempotency key) before deciding to compensate.

### Orchestration versus choreography

| | Orchestration | Choreography |
|---|---|---|
| Control | Central orchestrator | Services react to events |
| Visibility | Saga state in one place | Spread across services |
| Coupling | Orchestrator knows all | Services know events |
| Best for | Complex, many steps | Short, simple flows |

**Orchestration**: an orchestrator (a state machine, often built on Temporal, AWS Step Functions or Camunda) tells each service what to do and handles failures. The orchestrator's own state must be durable, so a crash mid-saga resumes where it left off; durable-execution engines like Temporal exist largely to provide that.

```
Orchestrator
 |--reserve stock--> Inventory
 |<--ok-------------
 |--charge---------> Payments
 |<--declined-------
 |--release stock--> Inventory
```

**Choreography**: each service publishes events and others subscribe. `OrderCreated` triggers Payments; `PaymentFailed` triggers Inventory to release stock and Orders to cancel. There's no central coordinator, but the flow is implicit and harder to trace or change, and cyclic dependencies creep in.

### Isolation: the saga's weakness

Sagas preserve local transaction guarantees but do not provide global ACID atomicity or isolation; compensation is a later business action, not an invisible rollback. Other transactions see intermediate states: a product shows "reserved" stock for an order that's about to be cancelled, or a balance briefly includes a charge that will be refunded. Anomalies include **lost updates** and **dirty reads** across steps. Countermeasures:

- **Semantic locks**: mark records as PENDING so others treat them carefully.
- **Commutative updates**: design steps so order doesn't matter (increment/decrement).
- **Re-reading values** before acting, or versioning records.

### Reliable messaging

Every step needs "update my database *and* publish an event" atomically, otherwise a crash between them stalls the saga. The standard fix is the **transactional outbox**: write the event to an `outbox` table in the same local transaction, and have a relay (or CDC tool like Debezium) publish it. Consumers must deduplicate, because delivery is at least once.

## Choosing

| Situation | Use |
|---|---|
| Shards of one database | 2PC over consensus groups |
| Few systems, short, need atomicity | 2PC/XA (carefully) |
| Microservices, long-running flow | Saga |
| Can redesign boundaries | Avoid it: one service owns the data |

## Key takeaways
- Atomic commit needs every participant to agree; one "no" aborts all, unlike majority consensus.
- 2PC: prepare (vote yes durably, keep locks) then commit; the coordinator's logged decision is the commit point.
- 2PC blocks if the coordinator fails after participants vote yes; they're in doubt, holding locks. A coordinator that restarts without a decision record presumes abort.
- 3PC avoids blocking only under synchronous assumptions; partitions break it. Real systems run 2PC with consensus-replicated coordinators.
- Sagas replace atomicity with local commits plus compensating transactions; order steps as compensatable, pivot, retriable.
- A timed-out step has an unknown outcome: compensations must handle steps that never ran, and late forward requests must be rejected.
- Orchestration centralises saga logic; choreography uses events. Sagas lack isolation, so use semantic locks and an outbox for reliable events.

questions.prompt: In two-phase commit, what does a participant promise when it votes **yes** to prepare?

options.text: That it has already committed the transaction.
options.explanation: Wrong. It hasn't committed yet; it's waiting for the coordinator's decision. Committing early would break atomicity if another participant votes no.

options.text: That it will commit if a majority of participants also vote yes.
options.explanation: Wrong. 2PC requires *all* participants to vote yes; majority voting is consensus, not atomic commit.

options.text: Nothing binding; it can still abort if it times out.
options.explanation: Wrong. Before voting it can abort freely; after a yes vote it can't, which is exactly what causes the blocking problem.

options.text: That it will commit if told to, even after a crash, so it has durably written the changes and keeps its locks.
options.explanation: Correct. A yes vote surrenders the right to abort unilaterally. The participant persists everything needed to commit and holds locks until it hears the decision.

questions.workedExample:
Lifecycle of a participant:

1. Executes the transaction's writes (uncommitted).
2. Receives PREPARE.
3. If able to commit: `fsync` changes + prepare record, then vote YES. Now **in doubt** until the decision.
4. Receives COMMIT or ABORT and applies it, releasing locks.

In Postgres, step 3 is `PREPARE TRANSACTION 'tx42'`; step 4 is `COMMIT PREPARED 'tx42'`.

questions.prompt: In 2PC with participants P1, P2 and P3: all three vote yes, the coordinator writes COMMIT to its log, sends commit to P1 only, then crashes. P2 and P3 time out waiting. What should P2 do?

options.text: Abort, since it never got a decision.
options.explanation: Wrong. The coordinator decided COMMIT and P1 already committed. Aborting P2 would break atomicity.

options.text: Stay in doubt holding locks; it may ask P1, and if P1 reports it committed, P2 can commit.
options.explanation: Correct. P2 must not decide alone. If it can reach a participant that knows the outcome (P1 committed), it can follow; otherwise it waits for the coordinator to recover.

options.text: Commit, since it voted yes.
options.explanation: Wrong as a general rule. Voting yes doesn't mean the decision was commit; another participant might have voted no. P2 only *happens* to be safe here if it can learn the outcome.

options.text: Ask P3 and follow the majority.
options.explanation: Wrong. P3 is also in doubt, so it knows nothing more. Majority vote among in-doubt participants doesn't reveal the coordinator's decision.

questions.workedExample:
1. Commit point = coordinator's COMMIT log record. Decision is **commit**.
2. P1 knows (it received commit).
3. P2 and P3 know only that *they* voted yes.
4. Options for P2:
  - Ask P1: 'I committed tx42' → P2 commits (cooperative termination).
  - If P1 is unreachable too: wait for the coordinator to restart, read its log, and resend COMMIT.
5. Meanwhile P2 holds locks; transactions touching those rows block. That's the **blocking problem**.

questions.prompt: Why isn't three-phase commit widely used to solve 2PC's blocking problem?

options.text: Its non-blocking guarantee assumes bounded delays and perfect failure detection; under a network partition, groups can reach different decisions.
options.explanation: Correct. Recovery relies on communication and failure-detection assumptions that a partition violates. Extra phases do not make arbitrary partitions safe and non-blocking.

options.text: It needs three coordinators.
options.explanation: Wrong. 3PC has one coordinator; the 'three' refers to message phases, not coordinators.

options.text: It's slower than sagas.
options.explanation: Wrong. Speed isn't the core problem; 3PC's flaw is safety under partitions, and sagas offer different (weaker) guarantees altogether.

options.text: It can't handle participants voting no.
options.explanation: Wrong. 3PC handles no votes just like 2PC: the coordinator aborts.

questions.workedExample:
1. 3PC adds a pre-commit state before the final commit decision.
2. After a coordinator failure, survivors exchange protocol states through a termination protocol; local phase alone is not permission to decide independently.
3. Under the assumed timing and failure model, this can complete without the failed coordinator.
4. A network partition prevents a reliable view of all surviving participants and invalidates the non-blocking safety argument. Replicating transaction state with consensus is the common practical alternative, but progress still needs reachable quorums.

questions.prompt: An order saga runs: (1) create order PENDING, (2) reserve stock, (3) charge card, (4) send confirmation email. Step 3 fails (card declined). What does the saga do?

options.text: Roll back the database transactions of steps 1 and 2.
options.explanation: Wrong. Steps 1 and 2 already committed in their own services; there's no open transaction to roll back. A saga undoes them with new compensating transactions.

options.text: Retry step 3 until it succeeds.
options.explanation: Wrong. A declined card is a business failure, not a transient error. Retrying forever won't help; only steps after the pivot should be retried to completion.

options.text: Run compensations in reverse: release the stock, then cancel the order.
options.explanation: Correct. Each completed step gets a semantic undo, executed in reverse order, while step 4 never runs.

options.text: Send the confirmation email, then refund.
options.explanation: Wrong. The email (step 4) shouldn't run because the saga failed before it; it's not compensatable, which is why it comes last.

questions.workedExample:
Steps and their compensations:

| Step | Compensation |
|---|---|
| T1 create order | C1 cancel order |
| T2 reserve stock | C2 release stock |
| T3 charge card (pivot) | – |
| T4 email (retriable) | – |

T3 fails, so: run **C2** (release), then **C1** (cancel). Each compensation is idempotent and retried until it succeeds. The customer sees 'payment declined, order cancelled'.

questions.prompt: Which statements about sagas are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: They provide isolation: other transactions never see intermediate states.
options.explanation: Wrong. Each local transaction commits immediately, so intermediate states (reserved stock, a charge that will be refunded) are visible. Sagas lack the I in ACID.

options.text: Compensating transactions must be idempotent.
options.explanation: Correct. Compensations are retried after timeouts or crashes; running a refund twice must not refund twice.

options.text: Non-compensatable actions should come after the pivot step.
options.explanation: Correct. Things like sending emails or shipping can't be undone, so they belong after the point of no return, as retriable steps.

options.text: Choreography makes the end-to-end flow easier to see and change than orchestration.
options.explanation: Wrong. Choreography spreads the flow across event subscriptions; orchestration keeps it in one state machine, which is easier to understand and change.

options.text: A transactional outbox prevents a service from committing its change without emitting the event.
options.explanation: Correct. The event is written in the same local transaction as the state change, then relayed, so a crash can't separate them.

questions.workedExample:
Check each claim against how sagas work:

1. Isolation: local commits are visible immediately. ✗
2. Idempotent compensations: needed because of retries. ✓
3. Step ordering: compensatable → pivot → retriable. ✓
4. Choreography visibility: the opposite is true. ✗
5. Outbox: atomic 'write + event' within one database. ✓

questions.prompt: How can consensus replication reduce 2PC blocking after an individual coordinator node crashes, provided the required groups retain reachable quorums?

options.text: They use 3PC instead.
options.explanation: Wrong. Neither uses 3PC; its partition behaviour is unsafe.

options.text: They skip the prepare phase for single-row writes only.
options.explanation: Wrong. Single-range optimisations exist, but that doesn't explain how multi-shard transactions avoid blocking.

options.text: They use sagas internally.
options.explanation: Wrong. Sagas give up atomicity and isolation; these databases provide serializable ACID transactions.

options.text: The coordinator and each participant are consensus-replicated groups, so a node failure triggers a leader election rather than losing the decision.
options.explanation: Correct. Replicated transaction state permits a surviving leader to recover the decision. Progress still requires the relevant quorums and participants to be reachable.

questions.workedExample:
The blocking problem arises because the decision lives on **one** coordinator machine.

1. Make the coordinator a Raft group of 3 or 5 replicas.
2. The COMMIT record is a Raft log entry, committed on a majority.
3. If the coordinator's leader crashes, a new leader is elected in seconds and already has the log.
4. It resumes sending COMMIT.

Participants are Raft groups too, so their prepared state is replicated. Progress can still block if a required quorum becomes unreachable, including a partition that leaves all machines running.

questions.prompt: In a choreographed saga, the Payments service updates its database to CHARGED and then publishes `PaymentSucceeded` to Kafka. It crashes between the two. What happens and what's the fix?

options.text: Kafka replays the message automatically; no fix needed.
options.explanation: Wrong. The message was never sent, so Kafka has nothing to replay.

options.text: The saga stalls: the customer is charged but no downstream service learns of it. Fix with a transactional outbox.
options.explanation: Correct. The database change committed but the event was lost. Writing the event to an outbox table in the same transaction, and relaying it, makes the two atomic.

options.text: The charge rolls back automatically.
options.explanation: Wrong. The local transaction committed before the crash; nothing undoes it.

options.text: Fix it by publishing first, then updating the database.
options.explanation: Wrong. That just reverses the failure: an event saying 'charged' with no record of the charge if the crash happens after publishing.

questions.prompt: A 2PC coordinator receives yes votes from both participants, then crashes **before** writing any decision record. It restarts and finds the transaction in its log with no COMMIT or ABORT. What should it do?

options.text: Commit, because both participants voted yes.
options.explanation: Wrong. It may not know that both votes arrived, and in any case the decision is only made when it's logged. With no record, the safe and conventional choice is abort.

options.text: Wait for an operator to decide.
options.explanation: Wrong. There is no ambiguity here. Without a decision record, no participant can have been told to commit, so aborting can't conflict with anything.

options.text: Abort (presumed abort): no participant can have been told to commit, so aborting is safe.
options.explanation: Correct. The commit point is the COMMIT log record. Since it was never written, nobody committed. The coordinator aborts and tells the in-doubt participants, which then release their locks.

options.text: Ask the participants to vote again.
options.explanation: Wrong. Participants that voted yes are already bound to their vote. Re-voting adds nothing, because the problem is the missing decision, not missing votes.

questions.workedExample:
1. Commit point = the coordinator's durable COMMIT record.
2. No record → the coordinator never reached the commit point.
3. It only sends COMMIT after logging it, so no participant has received COMMIT.
4. Therefore aborting can't contradict any participant. **Abort**, and send ABORT to everyone in doubt.

This is **presumed abort**: "no record means abort". It also saves work, because the coordinator doesn't need to force ABORT records to disk.

questions.prompt: An orchestrated saga calls Payments to charge £40 for order 77 with idempotency key `o77-charge`. The call times out, so the orchestrator compensates: it calls refund, Payments finds no charge, and returns OK. Ten seconds later, the original charge request, delayed in a queue, reaches Payments. How should the system be designed so the customer isn't charged for a cancelled order?

options.text: Retry the refund on a timer for an hour, in case a charge turns up.
options.explanation: Wrong. It narrows the window but doesn't close it, and the customer may still see a charge and a refund on their statement.

options.text: Make the forward step the pivot so it never needs compensating.
options.explanation: Wrong. Calling it the pivot doesn't change the fact that its outcome is unknown after a timeout; the saga still has to decide what to do.

options.text: It can't be prevented; this is an inherent weakness of sagas.
options.explanation: Wrong. It is preventable with careful design at the participant.

options.text: Payments records "o77-charge cancelled" when it handles the refund, and rejects any later charge with that key.
options.explanation: Correct. The participant records cancellation against the forward operation's identifier and rejects a late charge. The refund/cancellation API request has its own idempotency key; correlation and request deduplication are different roles.

questions.workedExample:
The race:

```
t=0   charge(o77) sent, delayed
t=5   timeout -> refund(o77)
      no charge found -> OK
t=15  charge(o77) arrives
```

Without a record of the refund, Payments would charge at t=15 and nothing would undo it.

Design rules:

1. The compensation must be safe if the forward step never ran (refund of nothing = no-op).
2. It must leave a durable record against the **same forward-operation identifier**, while using a distinct idempotency key for the compensation request, so the forward step arriving later is rejected.
3. Better still, before compensating, query the step's status by key.

questions.prompt: A travel-booking saga has four steps: hold a seat (can be released), charge the card, issue the e-ticket (can't be undone once sent to the airline), and email the itinerary. Which ordering follows the compensatable → pivot → retriable pattern?

options.text: Hold seat, charge card, issue ticket, email
options.explanation: Correct. The hold is compensatable, the charge is the pivot, and once it succeeds the ticket and email are retriable steps that must eventually succeed.

options.text: Issue ticket, hold seat, charge card, email
options.explanation: Wrong. Issuing the ticket first puts an irreversible step before anything that might fail, such as a declined card, with no way to undo it.

options.text: Email, hold seat, charge card, issue ticket
options.explanation: Wrong. Emailing an itinerary before you know the booking will succeed tells the customer something that may turn out to be false.

options.text: Charge card, hold seat, issue ticket, email
options.explanation: Wrong. Charging before holding the seat means a "no seats left" failure requires a refund, which is exactly the kind of messy compensation good ordering avoids.

questions.workedExample:
Classify each step:

| Step | Type |
|---|---|
| Hold seat | compensatable (release) |
| Charge card | pivot (go/no-go) |
| Issue ticket | retriable (can't undo) |
| Email | retriable |

Put everything that may fail for business reasons (no seat, card declined) **before** the pivot, so failures are undone cheaply. After the pivot, the saga only moves forward: ticket issuance and email are retried, idempotently, until they succeed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about two-phase commit are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: If a participant crashes before voting, the coordinator can safely abort the transaction.
options.explanation: True. No yes vote means no promise to commit, so the coordinator treats the missing vote as no and aborts.

options.text: A participant that crashes after voting yes must, on restart, stay in doubt and ask the coordinator for the outcome.
options.explanation: True. Its prepare record shows it promised to commit if told to. It can't abort on its own, and it doesn't know the decision, so it must find out.

options.text: If the coordinator crashes after logging COMMIT, in-doubt participants may safely abort after a timeout.
options.explanation: False. The decision was commit, and some participants may already have committed. Aborting would break atomicity.

options.text: While participants are in doubt, other transactions that need the same rows are blocked.
options.explanation: True. In-doubt participants keep their locks, so contention spreads the outage to unrelated transactions.

options.text: 2PC keeps working through a coordinator crash as long as a majority of participants are up.
options.explanation: False. Plain 2PC has no majority rule; the decision lives on the coordinator alone. Tolerating its failure needs a replicated (consensus-backed) coordinator.

questions.workedExample:
Walk through the failure cases:

1. **Participant fails before voting** → coordinator times out, aborts. ✓ safe.
2. **Participant fails after yes** → restarts in doubt from its prepare record. ✓
3. **Coordinator fails after COMMIT logged** → outcome is commit; participants must wait or learn it from a peer. Aborting is wrong. ✗
4. **In doubt** → locks held, others block. ✓
5. **Majority survival** → not a 2PC concept. ✗

The fix for 3 and 5 is the same: make the coordinator a Raft or Paxos group, as Spanner and CockroachDB do.

questions.prompt: A loan-approval process has nine steps across six services, with branches (manual review if a credit score is borderline), timeouts measured in days, and frequent rule changes. Which saga style fits best?

options.text: Choreography, because it avoids a central point of failure.
options.explanation: Wrong for this flow. With nine steps, branches and long timeouts, the logic would be spread across event subscriptions in six services, making it hard to see, test or change.

options.text: Orchestration, with durable state in a workflow engine such as Temporal or Step Functions.
options.explanation: Correct. One state machine holds the whole flow, including branches and long timers, so it's visible, testable and changeable in one place, and survives crashes by persisting its state.

options.text: 2PC across all six services.
options.explanation: Wrong. 2PC would hold locks across services for days while waiting for manual review; that's exactly what sagas exist to avoid.

options.text: No coordination: each service retries until the loan is approved.
options.explanation: Wrong. Without a saga there's no defined way to undo completed steps when a later one rejects the loan.

questions.workedExample:
Score the flow against the table in the lesson:

| Factor | Favours |
|---|---|
| 9 steps, 6 services | orchestration |
| Branches | orchestration |
| Day-long timers | durable orchestrator |
| Frequent changes | orchestration |

Choreography shines for short, stable flows of two or three steps. Here, a durable orchestrator keeps the saga's state in one place, can sleep for days on a timer, and resumes correctly after a crash.

lessons.title: Conflict resolution, CRDTs and gossip
lessons.summary: Resolving concurrent writes with last-write-wins, version vectors and CRDTs (G-Counter, PN-Counter, OR-Set), and spreading state with gossip, phi accrual and SWIM.
lessons.body:
Systems that accept writes on several replicas at once (multi-leader, leaderless, offline-first apps, multi-region active-active) will see **concurrent writes** to the same data. They must merge them so that every replica ends up with the same value. This lesson covers how, and how such clusters learn about each other through gossip.

## Detecting conflicts: version vectors

Before you resolve a conflict you need to know one exists. A **version vector** (a vector clock keyed by replica rather than by client) records, for each replica, how many updates from it this version has seen.

```
replica A writes:  {A:1}
replica B writes:  {A:1, B:1}  (saw A's)
replica A writes:  {A:2}       (didn't
                                see B's)
```

Compare `{A:1, B:1}` with `{A:2}`: each is ahead in one entry, so they're **concurrent**. A store like Riak keeps both as **siblings** and returns both to the next reader, who merges them and writes back with a vector that dominates both, `{A:2, B:1}` plus an increment.

If one vector dominates (≥ in every entry), the dominated version is simply obsolete and can be discarded.

## Last-write-wins (LWW)

The simplest resolution: attach a timestamp to every write and keep the highest (ties broken by something deterministic, such as replica id). Cassandra does this per column; DynamoDB global tables do it per item in their default, eventually consistent mode.

It's simple and converges, but it **silently loses data**:

- Two concurrent writes: one is discarded, even though both clients got "success".
- With clock skew, a write that happened later can lose to an earlier one with a faster clock.

```
t=10.000 A: cart = [book]   clock +50ms
t=10.020 B: cart = [pen]    clock ok
stored ts: A=10.050, B=10.020
LWW keeps [book]; [pen] lost
```

LWW is fine when writes are naturally immutable (each key written once, e.g. keyed by UUID) or when losing a concurrent update is acceptable (a user's "last seen" time). For anything like a shopping cart, you need a merge.

> [!example] Dynamo's shopping cart
> The Dynamo paper's cart merged siblings by taking the **union** of items. That never loses an add, but a removed item could reappear if a concurrent sibling still contained it. That's exactly the problem the OR-Set solves.

## CRDTs

A **Conflict-free Replicated Data Type** is a data structure designed so that replicas can be updated independently and **always merge to the same result**, with no coordination and no conflicts to resolve by hand.

State-based CRDTs (CvRDTs) define a `merge` function that is:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Commutative | merge(a, b) = merge(b, a) |
| Associative | Grouping doesn't matter |
| Idempotent | merge(a, a) = a |

Those three properties mean replicas can exchange state in any order, any number of times, via any path (gossip), and still converge. That's **strong eventual consistency**: replicas that have received the same updates are in the same state.

There's a fourth condition that's easy to miss: **local updates may only move the state "upwards"**, so that the updated state, merged with the old one, gives the updated state. Formally, states form a *join-semilattice*, merge is the least upper bound, and updates are inflationary. That's why a G-Counter may only increase entries and why a set "remove" is recorded as a tombstone rather than by deleting the element: a deletion would be undone by the next merge with a replica that still has it.

Operation-based CRDTs (CmRDTs) instead broadcast operations. Concurrent operations must commute, and the delivery layer usually has to deliver each operation **exactly once** and in **causal order**. They send less data but need more from the network. Delta-state CRDTs sit in between: they ship only the recently changed part of the state, merged with the same join.

### G-Counter (grow-only counter)

Each replica keeps a vector of counts, one per replica, and only increments its own entry.

- `increment()` on replica i: `P[i] += 1`
- `value()`: sum of all entries
- `merge(X, Y)`: element-wise max

```
A: [A:3, B:0, C:0]  (3 local incs)
B: [A:1, B:2, C:0]  (saw 1 of A's)
merge -> [A:3, B:2, C:0]
value = 5
```

Why max and not sum? Because merging the same state twice must not double count (idempotence). Each entry is only ever increased by its owner, so the max is always the owner's latest value.

### PN-Counter (increment and decrement)

A G-Counter can't decrement: lowering an entry would be undone by max. So use **two** G-Counters: `P` for increments and `N` for decrements.

- `value() = sum(P) − sum(N)`
- `merge` merges P and N separately.

```
A: P=[A:5,B:0] N=[A:1,B:0]
B: P=[A:2,B:3] N=[A:0,B:2]
merge:
P=[A:5,B:3] = 8
N=[A:1,B:2] = 3
value = 5
```

Used for like-counts, stock levels where brief overselling is tolerable, and Redis Enterprise's active-active counters. Note that a PN-Counter can't enforce "never below zero": that's a global invariant needing coordination.

A middle ground is an **escrow** (or bounded) counter: split the available stock between replicas up front (say 60 units to EU, 40 to US). Each replica can decrement its own share without coordination and only needs to talk to others to borrow more. The invariant holds, and coordination happens only near the limit.

### G-Set and 2P-Set

A **G-Set** only grows; merge is union. A **2P-Set** adds a "tombstone" set of removed elements; an element is present if it's in the add-set and not the remove-set. Its flaw: once removed, an element can **never be re-added**.

### OR-Set (observed-remove set)

The OR-Set fixes that. Every `add(x)` attaches a **unique tag** (e.g. replica id + counter). `remove(x)` removes only the tags the remover has **observed**.

```
A: add(milk) tag a1
   -> sync to B
B: remove(milk)  removes {a1}
A: add(milk) tag a2   (concurrent)
merge:
 adds   = {a1, a2}
 removes= {a1}
 milk present (tag a2 survives)
```

Concurrent add and remove resolves to **add wins**, which is usually what users expect (re-adding milk to the shopping list shouldn't be cancelled by someone else's earlier removal). Riak's sets and maps, Redis CRDB sets and Automerge's internals use this idea.

### Beyond sets

- **LWW-Register / MV-Register**: a single value, resolved by timestamp or kept as multiple values.
- **Maps** of CRDTs, recursively.
- **Sequence CRDTs** (RGA, Logoot, Yjs, Automerge) for collaborative text editing, as in many real-time editors.

Costs: metadata grows (tags and tombstones accumulate and need garbage collection). Arbitrary independent updates cannot preserve every invariant; bounded counters can enforce non-negative stock using preallocated rights, as described above.

Garbage collection is the hard part. A tombstone can only be dropped once **every** replica has seen it; otherwise a replica that was offline still holds the old add, and the next merge brings the element back. Knowing that every replica has caught up is itself a coordination problem, the same one behind Cassandra's `gc_grace_seconds` in lesson 4. (Optimised OR-Sets such as Riak's ORSWOT avoid most tombstones by using version vectors, but pay in vector size instead.)

> [!tip] Choosing
> Use a CRDT when merging is semantically clear (counters, sets, collaborative docs) and availability matters more than invariants. Use consensus when you need invariants.

## Gossip protocols

Large clusters (Cassandra, Consul, Riak, ScyllaDB) need every node to learn membership, liveness and metadata without a central server. **Gossip** (epidemic) protocols do this:

1. Every interval (e.g. 1 s), each node picks a random peer (or a few).
2. They exchange state digests and the newer entries (push, pull or push-pull).
3. Information spreads like an infection.

```
round 0: 1 node knows
round 1: 2
round 2: 4
round 3: 8 ...
~log2(N) rounds to reach most
```

The doubling picture is the optimistic phase. Because peers are picked at random, more and more messages land on nodes that already know, and the last few uninformed nodes take a while to be hit. For push gossip with fanout 1 the total is about log₂N + ln N rounds: with N = 1,000 that's roughly 10 + 7 ≈ 17 rounds. Push-pull (where uninformed nodes also *ask* random peers) finishes the tail much faster. Either way it's O(log N).

Load per node is constant regardless of cluster size, and gossip tolerates node and message loss naturally. CRDT merges pair well with gossip because they're idempotent and order-insensitive.

## Failure detection

### Heartbeats with a fixed timeout

The simplest detector: if no heartbeat for T seconds, mark dead. Pick T too short and you get false positives under load; too long and real failures go unnoticed. One threshold can't suit every network condition.

### Phi accrual failure detector

Hayashibara et al. (2004), used by Cassandra and Akka, output a **suspicion level φ** instead of a yes/no.

- Each node records recent heartbeat inter-arrival times and models them as a distribution (the original paper uses a normal distribution with the observed mean and variance; Cassandra uses a simpler exponential model).
- φ = −log₁₀(P(a heartbeat arrives later than now)).

| φ | Modelled heartbeat tail probability |
|---|---|
| 1 | 10% |
| 3 | 0.1% |
| 8 | 0.000001% |

The application chooses a threshold (Cassandra's `phi_convict_threshold` defaults to 8). The adaptation depends on the model: Cassandra's exponential detector uses the observed mean interval, so extra variance alone at the same mean does not guarantee later conviction. The tail probability is not a measured false-positive rate.

### SWIM

SWIM (Das, Gupta and Motivala, 2002) is a scalable membership protocol, used in HashiCorp's memberlist (Consul, Nomad, Serf).

```
A             B          C (helpers)
|--ping------>X
| no ack in time
|--ping-req(B)--------->C
               C--ping->B
               C<--ack--B
|<-------ack------------C
B is alive (A's path was bad)
```

1. Each period, A pings one random member B.
2. No ack? A asks k other members to **ping-req** B on its behalf (indirect probing), which rules out a problem with A's own link.
3. Still nothing: B is **suspected**, not dead. Suspicion is gossiped; B can refute it by gossiping an incremented **incarnation number**.
4. After a suspicion timeout, B is declared **dead**.

Membership updates **piggyback** on ping and ack messages, so there's no separate broadcast traffic. Per-node load is constant and detection time doesn't grow with cluster size. HashiCorp's Lifeguard extensions further reduce false positives from slow, overloaded nodes.

## Key takeaways
- Version vectors detect concurrent writes; dominated versions are discarded, concurrent ones become siblings to merge.
- Last-write-wins is simple but silently drops concurrent writes and is vulnerable to clock skew; use it only for immutable or unimportant data.
- CRDT merges are commutative, associative and idempotent, and updates only move state upwards in the lattice, giving strong eventual consistency without coordination.
- G-Counter merges with element-wise max; PN-Counter pairs two G-Counters; OR-Set tags each add so concurrent add and remove resolves to add-wins.
- CRDTs cannot preserve arbitrary global invariants under unrestricted updates and can accumulate metadata; garbage-collecting tombstones needs every replica to have caught up. Use consensus (or escrow) where invariants matter.
- Gossip spreads state in O(log N) rounds (about log₂N + ln N for push) with constant per-node load; phi accrual gives adaptive suspicion levels; SWIM adds indirect probes and suspicion with incarnation numbers.

questions.prompt: Two users edit the same shopping cart on different replicas at the same moment: one adds a book, the other adds a pen. The store uses **last-write-wins**. What happens?

options.text: One of the additions is silently lost.
options.explanation: Correct. Each write replaces the whole cart; the one with the lower timestamp is discarded, even though both clients were told their write succeeded.

options.text: The cart contains both items.
options.explanation: Wrong. LWW keeps one whole value (the one with the higher timestamp) and discards the other; it doesn't merge.

options.text: Both writes fail with a conflict error.
options.explanation: Wrong. LWW never reports conflicts; it resolves them automatically by timestamp. That's its appeal and its danger.

options.text: The store keeps both carts as siblings.
options.explanation: Wrong. Keeping siblings is what version-vector stores like Riak do; LWW throws one away.

questions.workedExample:
1. Replica A: cart = [book], ts = 10.050.
2. Replica B: cart = [pen], ts = 10.020.
3. Replication: both see both versions; LWW keeps max ts → [book].
4. The pen is gone, and neither user was told.

Better: model the cart as an OR-Set CRDT so the merge is [book, pen].

questions.prompt: A G-Counter has three replicas. Their states are A = [A:4, B:1, C:0], B = [A:2, B:3, C:0], C = [A:3, B:1, C:2]. After all three merge, what is the counter's value?

options.explanation: Wrong. That sums every entry across all three states, which double counts increments seen by more than one replica.
Wrong. 7 isn't the value of any consistent state: replica A alone is 5 and C alone is 6. The merged state takes the max of every entry, giving 9.
Wrong. That's just replica A's value (4 + 1 + 0). It ignores B's and C's newer local increments.
Correct. Element-wise max gives [A:4, B:3, C:2], and 4 + 3 + 2 = 9.

questions.workedExample:
Merge = element-wise max:

| | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| A's state | 4 | 1 | 0 |
| B's state | 2 | 3 | 0 |
| C's state | 3 | 1 | 2 |
| **max** | **4** | **3** | **2** |

Value = 4 + 3 + 2 = **9**.

Each entry is only ever incremented by its owner, so the max is that owner's true count. Summing would count A's increments up to three times.

questions.prompt: Why can't you implement decrement on a G-Counter by simply lowering your own entry?

options.text: Because negative numbers aren't allowed in vectors.
options.explanation: Wrong. Lowering from 5 to 4 isn't negative; the real problem is the merge function.

options.text: Because the merge takes the element-wise max, so the lower value would be overwritten by any replica holding the old, higher one.
options.explanation: Correct. Max-merge only lets values grow. A decrement would be undone the moment you merged with a replica that saw the pre-decrement value. Hence PN-Counter's separate N vector.

options.text: Because decrements need consensus.
options.explanation: Wrong. PN-Counters support decrements without consensus. Only invariants like 'never below zero' need coordination.

options.text: Because the sum would overflow.
options.explanation: Wrong. Overflow isn't related; the issue is that max-merge isn't compatible with decreasing values.

questions.workedExample:
1. A = [A:5], gossips to B. B = [A:5].
2. A decrements by lowering: A = [A:4].
3. Merge(A, B) = [max(4, 5)] = [A:5]. The decrement vanished.

PN-Counter fix: keep P = [A:5] and N = [A:1]. Both only grow, so max-merge is correct. Value = 5 − 1 = 4.

questions.prompt: In an **OR-Set**, replica A adds "milk" (tag a1) and syncs to B. Then, concurrently, B removes "milk" and A adds "milk" again (tag a2). After they merge, is milk in the set?

options.text: Yes: tag a2 was never observed by the remove, so it survives (add wins).
options.explanation: Correct. The merged add-set is {a1, a2}, the remove-set is {a1}, leaving a2. Concurrent add and remove resolve to add-wins.

options.text: No: the remove happened, so milk is gone.
options.explanation: Wrong. B's remove only removes tags B had observed, i.e. a1. It can't remove a2, which it never saw.

options.text: It depends on which operation had the higher timestamp.
options.explanation: Wrong. OR-Sets don't use timestamps at all; that's an LWW-Element-Set. Resolution comes from observed tags.

options.text: The merge fails and needs manual resolution.
options.explanation: Wrong. CRDTs by definition always merge automatically and deterministically.

questions.workedExample:
Track tags:

1. A: add(milk, a1). Sync → B sees {a1}.
2. B: remove(milk) → tombstones the tags it sees: {a1}.
3. A (concurrently): add(milk, a2).
4. Merge:
  - adds = {a1, a2}
  - removed = {a1}
  - live = {a2} → milk **present**.

A 2P-Set would have said 'removed forever'. The OR-Set's unique tags let re-adds survive.
